== <span class="c5">Protestant Reformation and the Turn from Ritual to Belief</span> ==
<span class="c7 c8">Introduction.</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;The Protestant Reformation did not merely reinterpret Christian doctrine; it </span><span class="c7 c8">recast the very structure of religious life</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;in early modern Europe. In predominantly Catholic medieval Europe, &ldquo;embodied&rdquo; religion centered on communal ritual, sacramental symbols, and mythic cosmologies (the saints, the Mass as sacrifice, pilgrimages, indulgences, etc.). Protestantism, by contrast, prized </span><span class="c1">inner faith</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">&nbsp;and Scripture, subordinating outward ceremony to personal conviction and doctrine. This shift can be seen as a flattening of the old mythic order into a self&#8209;enclosed, rationalized belief system. We analyze this transformation through a post-structuralist lens (especially Foucault&rsquo;s concept of discipline and power) while drawing on sociology (Weber&rsquo;s Protestant Ethic), intellectual history (Taylor on secular experience), and political economy (the reallocation of church wealth). Each section addresses one facet of the Reformation&rsquo;s restructuring of religion.</span>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Economic Entanglements: Reformation and Early Capitalism</span> ===
<span class="c7">The Reformation emerged amid the breakdown of feudal order and the rise of commercial capitalism. As Cantoni </span><span class="c1">et al.</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;demonstrate, </span><span class="c7 c8">massive resources</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(land, wealth, human capital) shifted from ecclesiastical to secular hands. Closed monasteries and confiscated church lands funded palaces, roads, and civic institutions in Protestant territories</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3DUsing%2520novel%2520microdata%252C%2520we%2520document,This%2520transfer%2520of%2520resources%2520had&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805528279&amp;usg=AOvVaw0PI4WK8vXe1WFLNKayc9y-">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c7">. Cantoni, Dittmar, and Yuchtman (2017) find that &ldquo;secular authorities acquired enormous amounts of wealth from monasteries closed during the Reformation,&rdquo; and that Protestant regions saw new investment in non&#8209;religious buildings (palaces, town halls)</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3DUsing%2520novel%2520microdata%252C%2520we%2520document,This%2520transfer%2520of%2520resources%2520had&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805528831&amp;usg=AOvVaw0Ur-v35BZHIwywFBFPOA3g">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3Dfor%2520public%2520sector%2520jobs%252C%2520rather,the%2520secularization%2520of%2520the%2520West&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805528988&amp;usg=AOvVaw2sIcwWfPxMYKTN8zlpsTcm">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c7">. This &ldquo;reallocation&rdquo; of resources </span><span class="c7 c8">powered emerging bourgeois classes</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;and civil bureaucracy (many graduates of Protestant universities went into public service</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3Dacquired%2520enormous%2520amounts%2520of%2520wealth,palaces%2520and%2520administrative%2520buildings%252C%2520which&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805529567&amp;usg=AOvVaw2G1T0rc0-fJKzjlh6jOA1v">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c7">). In short, Protestant reform created an economic base for capitalist society by </span><span class="c7 c8">diverting church rent&#8209;seeking into profit&#8209;seeking and state formation</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3DUsing%2520novel%2520microdata%252C%2520we%2520document,This%2520transfer%2520of%2520resources%2520had&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805529976&amp;usg=AOvVaw3_UqrWBzlws0-3Nrn03GG6">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3Dfor%2520public%2520sector%2520jobs%252C%2520rather,the%2520secularization%2520of%2520the%2520West&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805530184&amp;usg=AOvVaw3WjvHsbkowgUCEsmgDSKEm">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">.</span>

<span class="c7">Max Weber&rsquo;s classic analysis similarly links Protestant doctrine to capitalist subjectivity. Weber noted that </span><span class="c1">inner-worldly asceticism</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;&ndash; the &ldquo;calling&rdquo; or Beruf &ndash; was given a religious stamp by Luther and especially Calvin</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://anthropolojamz.wordpress.com/2015/10/11/weber-the-protestant-ethic-and-the-spirit-of-capitalism/%23:~:text%3DLuther%25E2%2580%2599s%2520Concept%2520of%2520the%2520Calling&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805530870&amp;usg=AOvVaw3BFLAdQvyjZy19KDhGy1iX">anthropolojamz.wordpress.com</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3D%25E2%2580%25A2,control%2520of%2520the%2520individual%2520which&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805531085&amp;usg=AOvVaw1pCBeyB55XlqtDblpSjeob">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c7">. Luther proclaimed in </span><span class="c1">On Christian Liberty</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(1520) that &ldquo;A Christian man is the most free lord of all, and subject to none; [yet] a Christian man is the most dutiful servant of all, and subject to every one&rdquo;</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://ccel.org/ccel/luther/christianliberty/christianliberty.iii.html%23:~:text%3Dspiritual%2520liberty%2520and%2520servitude%253A%25E2%2580%2594&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805531538&amp;usg=AOvVaw1Z12JAeYP6Qdz5mp-SaXYS">ccel.org</ref></span><span class="c7">. This paradoxical doctrine of inner freedom under God laid the groundwork for a self&#8209;disciplined individual. Calvin in Geneva demanded a &ldquo;monastic discipline for everyone,&rdquo; harnessing civic life to a rigorous piety</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://tif.ssrc.org/2007/10/19/secularism-of-a-new-kind/%23:~:text%3DTaylor%2520argues%2520that%2520the%2520Reformation%25E2%2580%2594with,with%2520its%2520emphasis%2520on%2520progress&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805531956&amp;usg=AOvVaw38uJfXwUxlAzUuxGy53S14">tif.ssrc.org</ref></span><span class="c7">. Weber argued that these Protestant innovations in conscience and labor discipline fostered &ldquo;the spirit of capitalism&rdquo;: hard work and reinvestment became seen as moral duties</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://anthropolojamz.wordpress.com/2015/10/11/weber-the-protestant-ethic-and-the-spirit-of-capitalism/%23:~:text%3D,dominated%2520by%2520the%2520making%2520of&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805532405&amp;usg=AOvVaw2ygKcodtZyCo98hYyiSDfg">anthropolojamz.wordpress.com</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://anthropolojamz.wordpress.com/2015/10/11/weber-the-protestant-ethic-and-the-spirit-of-capitalism/%23:~:text%3DLuther%25E2%2580%2599s%2520Concept%2520of%2520the%2520Calling&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805532657&amp;usg=AOvVaw3rtaWNjZgUdwYOnu5H6_mn">anthropolojamz.wordpress.com</ref></span><span class="c7">. In Weber&rsquo;s words, Calvinism created &ldquo;the most absolutely unbearable form of ecclesiastical control of the individual&rdquo;</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3Dthose%2520most%2520favorable%2520to%2520a,Tawney%2520%2528in%2520the&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805533045&amp;usg=AOvVaw2VBaEwfAxMBAAm482OZdmu">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c7">&nbsp;&ndash; a control that paradoxically </span><span class="c7 c8">channelled people&rsquo;s energies into industrious worldly activity</span><span class="c7">. Thus the Reformation&rsquo;s spirituality &ndash; </span><span class="c1">sola fide</span><span class="c7">, calling, worldly asceticism &ndash; intertwined with and advanced the rise of bourgeois wealth and individualist subjectivity</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3D%25E2%2580%25A2,control%2520of%2520the%2520individual%2520which&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805533639&amp;usg=AOvVaw2BtPgpdvylTDRUCuRuI4tb">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://ccel.org/ccel/luther/christianliberty/christianliberty.iii.html%23:~:text%3Dspiritual%2520liberty%2520and%2520servitude%253A%25E2%2580%2594&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805533790&amp;usg=AOvVaw0C1GpuKR4ClvJUFk_MQBoS">ccel.org</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">.</span>

<span class="c7">Moreover, Protestant political theory often justified the sovereign taking the place of the church. In the Holy Roman Empire, </span><span class="c1">cuius regio, eius religio</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(1555) allowed princes to seize former Catholic lands and impose state churches. Cantoni </span><span class="c1">et al.</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;note that this secularizing impulse was unintended but profound: Protestant &ldquo;entry&rdquo; was facilitated by emergent market societies willing to bear wealth into new &ldquo;utility-maximizing&rdquo; (in their terminology) contractual relations</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3Dhomoge%2502neous%2520event,absolutely%2520decisive%2520difference%2520from%2520Catholicism&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805534647&amp;usg=AOvVaw3UR2OSLlehdPfUrPjTnoBX">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3DUsing%2520novel%2520microdata%252C%2520we%2520document,This%2520transfer%2520of%2520resources%2520had&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805534808&amp;usg=AOvVaw2r9GEunBEZ2PK3ffx1qBsE">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c7">. In plain terms, where commerce thrived and the landed order weakened, both peasants and patricians found Lutheranism attractive &ndash; partly because it freed them from clerical tithes and obligations</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3D%25E2%2580%25A2,control%2520of%2520the%2520individual%2520which&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805535200&amp;usg=AOvVaw1_yfPu5YZAwfCOVBMqkguM">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3DUsing%2520novel%2520microdata%252C%2520we%2520document,This%2520transfer%2520of%2520resources%2520had&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805535372&amp;usg=AOvVaw3jNMqqTwxZNWiru48LdAaa">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c7">. By contrast, in stagnant feudal regions with strong nobility, the medieval Church could sustain its monopoly via patronage. Thus the Reformation both reflected and accelerated class realignments: it fostered </span><span class="c1">bourgeois subjectivities</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;of independent selfhood and profit&#8209;oriented discipline at the expense of feudal communalism</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3D%25E2%2580%25A2,control%2520of%2520the%2520individual%2520which&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805535940&amp;usg=AOvVaw2QW8Q57kpz1Pqr9IBMBEpV">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3DUsing%2520novel%2520microdata%252C%2520we%2520document,This%2520transfer%2520of%2520resources%2520had&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805536095&amp;usg=AOvVaw0R9qb5H2ntU_m7hjdLYsCi">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">.</span>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Iconoclasm and Ritual Decoding</span> ===
<span class="c7">Protestant reformers launched an explicit attack on </span><span class="c7 c8">Catholic ritual and imagery</span><span class="c7">. Initially, this took the form of iconoclasm: the mass destruction of statues, altars, and stained glass in many German, Swiss, and Dutch cities. Luther himself tolerated some images, but Zwingli and Calvin often proclaimed them &ldquo;idols,&rdquo; to be purged. As one recent study notes, modern aesthetic theories of image and art were </span><span class="c1">shaped</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;by the Reformation&rsquo;s iconophobia. Protestants and Counter-Reformation Catholics together &ldquo;exhib[ited] iconophilic and iconophobic aspects,&rdquo; and Protestant iconoclasm in the 1520s &ldquo;had a strong influence&rdquo; on later European views of imagesdiva-portal.org</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://politicaltheology.com/jean-luc-nancy/%23:~:text%3DA%2520world%2520without%2520God%2520is,all%2520is%2520dethroned%2520but%2520capital&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805537305&amp;usg=AOvVaw3RSzCKs9sfGKyJqxtVuLWl">politicaltheology.com</ref></span><span class="c7">. In practice this meant that </span><span class="c7 c8">mythic symbolism was stripped bare</span><span class="c7">. Where medieval churchgoers learned theology through ritual drama and icon, Protestant worship became &ldquo;instructive&rdquo;: centered on preaching and singing, in the vernacular, with an emphasis on plain clarity</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.catholicworldreport.com/2017/10/11/protestantism-in-the-catholic-church-the-emergence-of-a-shared-tradition/%23:~:text%3Dthat%2520have%2520influenced%2520the%2520way,of%2520Christ%2520over%2520these%2520elements&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805537855&amp;usg=AOvVaw0NEZf1DbCkMD-NlyFyhOl2">catholicworldreport.com</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.catholicworldreport.com/2017/10/11/protestantism-in-the-catholic-church-the-emergence-of-a-shared-tradition/%23:~:text%3Dthat%2520have%2520influenced%2520the%2520way,and%2520the%2520instructive%2520nature%2520of&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805538062&amp;usg=AOvVaw2LUL4lcBNb4Efk74BW5wm8">catholicworldreport.com</ref></span><span class="c7">. As a Catholic commentator observes, Protestant liturgy &ldquo;emphasizes clarity and simplicity over mystery and complex ritual&rdquo; &ndash; congregants now saw sermons rather than a sacred sacrifice, and ministers faced the people rather than leading esoteric rites</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.catholicworldreport.com/2017/10/11/protestantism-in-the-catholic-church-the-emergence-of-a-shared-tradition/%23:~:text%3Dthat%2520have%2520influenced%2520the%2520way,of%2520Christ%2520over%2520these%2520elements&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805538550&amp;usg=AOvVaw1-Wm-4e-Jx9DIGhXJH0N5H">catholicworldreport.com</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">.</span>

<span class="c7">This was more than aesthetic: the underlying theology reinterpreted every sacramental and seasonal symbol. The Mass ceased to be viewed as a mystical reenactment of Calvary; instead it became a commemorative Lord&rsquo;s Supper. Zwingli famously argued that Christ&rsquo;s presence in Communion is spiritual, not corporeal &ndash; a &ldquo;memorial&rdquo; meal for the faithful, not a magical transformation of bread. Luther retained a real presence but rescinded the Catholic notion of </span><span class="c1">transubstantiation</span><span class="c7">; Calvin spoke of a &ldquo;mystical presence&rdquo; but likewise rejected a physical sacrifice</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://oxfordre.com/religion/display/10.1093/acrefore/9780199340378.001.0001/acrefore-9780199340378-e-375?p%3DemailAwV26k/57IYO.%26d%3D/10.1093/acrefore/9780199340378.001.0001/acrefore-9780199340378-e-375%23:~:text%3DFor%2520Luther%252C%2520the%2520Supper%2520is,consists%2520of%2520the%2520participant%2527s&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805539521&amp;usg=AOvVaw02IU2_N76nN2x0dP2WqfnL">oxfordre.com</ref></span><span class="c7">. In effect, </span><span class="c7 c8">ritual time was flattened</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">&nbsp;into Scripture: saints&rsquo; days and feast-days were often abandoned (except, say, Christmas and Easter) in favor of the Sunday sermon. Liturgical calendar and sacramental seasons gave way to the printed Bible read on a weekly cycle.</span>

<span class="c7">From a post-structuralist view, this was a &ldquo;decoding&rdquo; of mythic signs into propositional content. Jean-Luc Nancy points out that monotheism has always &ldquo;withdrawn any myth or meaning from the world,&rdquo; positing a God removed from history</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://politicaltheology.com/jean-luc-nancy/%23:~:text%3Dorigins%2520of%2520the%2520West,rigorous%2520atheism%2520has%2520religious%2520roots&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805540315&amp;usg=AOvVaw0o4jQFpvZd0XJze1cpx9h_">politicaltheology.com</ref></span><span class="c7">. Protestantism extended this logic: the divine was accessible only in the </span><span class="c1">unmediated</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;Word. As Nancy writes, modernity&rsquo;s drive toward demythologization &ndash; stripping narrative out of social life &ldquo;in the name of &hellip; reason [or] progress&rdquo; &ndash; actually stems from this &ldquo;atheistic logic of monotheism&rdquo;</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://politicaltheology.com/jean-luc-nancy/%23:~:text%3DA%2520world%2520without%2520God%2520is,all%2520is%2520dethroned%2520but%2520capital&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805540798&amp;usg=AOvVaw3UMz34vMKUSRYMqAwYWAW7">politicaltheology.com</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">. In other words, Protestantism&rsquo;s assault on religious symbol was not against superstition alone but part of a deeper secularizing trajectory. Iconoclasm &ldquo;dismantled&rdquo; the old cosmos of signs so thoroughly that believers could only narrate history (biblical or moral) rather than feel mythic presence.</span>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">From Utopia to Discipline: Radical Sectarianism and Control</span> ===
<span class="c7">The Reformation unleashed utopian fervors, yet the Protestant mainstream quickly </span><span class="c7 c8">reined them in</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;through political alliance and social discipline. Radical sects (Anabaptists, Munsterites, Familists, Spiritualists, etc.) envisioned Christian communities based on shared goods, visions of imminent apocalypse, and direct revelation. These were </span><span class="c1">utopian</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;projects &ndash; calls to remake society along egalitarian or mystical lines. For example, M&uuml;nster (1534&ndash;35) briefly became an Anabaptist &ldquo;New Jerusalem,&rdquo; complete with communal property and polygamy under self-styled &ldquo;King David&rdquo; Jan van Leyden</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://gameo.org/index.php?title%3DM%25C3%25BCnster_Anabaptists%23:~:text%3Dbeen%2520sent%2520to%2520M%25C3%25BCnster%2520by,Others%2520were&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805542244&amp;usg=AOvVaw2rdxhXzVqDJDCuMwIh4513">gameo.org</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://gameo.org/index.php?title%3DM%25C3%25BCnster_Anabaptists%23:~:text%3DIn%2520addition%2520to%2520armed%2520resistance%252C,reading%2520Anabaptists&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805542416&amp;usg=AOvVaw1253lWfygPxHslyMGLDlq9">gameo.org</ref></span><span class="c7">. One historian notes that M&uuml;nster &ldquo;became the refuge of all persecuted, desperate people and the &lsquo;New Jerusalem&rsquo; of radical Anabaptism,&rdquo; drawing oppressed believers across Europe</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://gameo.org/index.php?title%3DM%25C3%25BCnster_Anabaptists%23:~:text%3Dbeen%2520sent%2520to%2520M%25C3%25BCnster%2520by,Others%2520were&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805542754&amp;usg=AOvVaw1nRDmORx5MkdMCXjKHf_go">gameo.org</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">. The city was besieged by the bishop&rsquo;s troops and retaken amid horrific carnage. With M&uuml;nster&rsquo;s fall, authorities in Protestant cities grew determined to suppress any communal experiment that threatened order.</span>

<span class="c7">Why this turn from utopia to discipline? Partly because secular rulers (both Protestant princes and Catholic emperors) saw the economic and political threat these sects posed. Elders who repudiated private property or refused to swear loyalty to princes challenged the emerging territorial states. Thus Anabaptists were soon banned by both Protestant and Catholic magistrates; M&uuml;nster&rsquo;s leaders were tortured and executed as a warning. The mainstream reformers (Lutherans, Reformed) largely </span><span class="c7 c8">disavowed</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">&nbsp;the radicals. Luther condemned peasant revolts (1525) on theological grounds, urging princes to &ldquo;slay even his father and mother&rdquo; if they rebelled against order (a brutal stance to preserve peace). The Reformed in Zurich executed Anabaptists as heretics (e.g. Michael Sattler in 1527). In England and Scandinavia, even moderate Protestants under monarchy outlawed sects that undermined royal control of the church.</span>

<span class="c7">This &ldquo;re-disciplining&rdquo; of utopian excess can be read through Foucault&rsquo;s lens of power and subjectivation. Lindholm and Di Carlo (2024) argue that early Lutheranism already displayed </span><span class="c7 c8">disciplinary power</span><span class="c7">: church services functioned like classrooms, training obedient subjects. In a famous Wittenberg altarpiece (by Cranach), Luther preaches from a pulpit to rapt congregants &ndash; a tableau much like Foucault&rsquo;s classroom illustration of surveillance and normalization. Here the minister </span><span class="c1">is</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;the teacher; the congregation </span><span class="c1">is</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;the disciplined class learning not Latin prayers but a doctrine. Foucault&rsquo;s concept of anatomo-politics applies: the Reformation increasingly positioned each soul under watchful guidance of preaching, catechism, and moral &ldquo;calling.&rdquo; By the mid-1500s, Protestant pastors and consistories oversaw schooling, poor relief, and even punishments for sins like adultery or Sabbath-breaking. Paradoxically, Protestants who celebrated individual faith also created tighter social regimentation &ndash; what Weber and others called &ldquo;the iron cage&rdquo; of discipline &ndash; to prevent heterodox alternatives</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3Dthose%2520most%2520favorable%2520to%2520a,Tawney%2520%2528in%2520the&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805545404&amp;usg=AOvVaw0KG7bRdCfvnybpK_mncFIc">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">.</span>

<span class="c7">Thus, liberal utopian energies were turned inward or bureaucratized. Public ecstatic prophecy gave way to private moral introspection. Where radicals preached overthrow of old orders, established Protestants preached obedience to magistrates (as a divine ordinance). Economic self-help replaced communal sharing (apart from groups like the Hutterites, who were also soon hunted). In short, </span><span class="c7 c8">utopian fervor was domesticated</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">: Protestant regimes curbed &ldquo;excess&rdquo; liberty by binding believers into state churches and market roles &ndash; a process very much in keeping with Foucault&rsquo;s genealogy of modern discipline.</span>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Sacramental Collapse: Demystifying the Cosmos</span> ===
<span class="c7">Central to Catholic Christianity was a </span><span class="c7 c8">sacramental worldview</span><span class="c7">: God&rsquo;s grace was mediated through visible rites and sacred objects. Transubstantiation, baptismal regeneration, confession, ordination, relics, and indulgences made the divine tangible. Protestantism, however, systematically </span><span class="c1">collapsed</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;this sacramental universe into scripture and conscience. Catholic salvation was communal and mystical; Protestant salvation was individual and textual. As Weber observed, the Lutheran Reformation &ldquo;completely eliminated salvation through Church and sacraments,&rdquo; redefining faith as a personal relation with Christ</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3Dhomoge%2502neous%2520event,absolutely%2520decisive%2520difference%2520from%2520Catholicism&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805547440&amp;usg=AOvVaw3U3j8nn_Gjmr3HZ5QgYnLJ">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">.</span>

<span class="c13 c7 c20">What was lost or transformed? The Catholic cosmos &ndash; a vertical ordering of Heaven, Earth, and the underworld &ndash; was flattened. Purgatory vanished (Protestants abolished indulgences and the treasury of merit), so the uncertainty of souls after death was replaced by assurance of personal salvation or damnation. The Mass was no longer seen as a propitiatory sacrifice transcending time; it became a &ldquo;supper&rdquo; of remembrance. Calvin even likened the Lord&rsquo;s Supper to the daily bread we eat &ndash; a simple, earthly sign of Christ&rsquo;s hidden presence. Some Protestants went further: Zwingli and the radical Anabaptists denied any real presence, treating Communion purely as a communal prayer. Thus &ldquo;mystery&rdquo; was deflated: nothing in the elements itself was magically efficacious, only faith made them meaningful.</span>

<span class="c7">On the one hand, this might look like </span><span class="c7 c8">demystification</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">. Protestant theology insisted on rational grounds: sacraments work when attended by true faith, not by any mystical power in the rite itself. Baptism, for example, was redefined as a sign of a covenant already bestowed by God, not as a merit-conferring act. In Protestant confessions, clergy are sharply demoted: there is no sacramental priesthood interposing between believer and God. Even Mary and the saints were largely excised from public worship (no more Corpus Christi or All Saints parades). What Foucault calls the &ldquo;pastoral&rdquo; function moved from confession to sermon and from the confessional stall to the bedroom: each believer&rsquo;s conscience became the locus of spiritual accountability.</span>

<span class="c7">On the other hand, Protestants redirected what had been &ldquo;sacred power&rdquo; into the Bible and the church as institution. With papal authority gone, scripture (and its interpretation by magisterial churches) became the ultimate arbiter of truth. One might say the church became its own miracle: words on a page, universally accessible, now held a quasi-cosmic primacy. Rather than relics or icons, Protestants prized the printed Word. Calvin&rsquo;s Geneva even instituted a sort of &ldquo;church discipline&rdquo; with courts enforcing Sunday worship and Biblical ethics &ndash; a new metaphysical order built on biblical time. In effect, sacraments were replaced by </span><span class="c1">proclamation</span><span class="c7">. Saving grace did not cease to exist; it was reimagined as fully present in the Word made flesh, accessible to all believers in community. This reconfiguration signaled a </span><span class="c1">redirection</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;of spiritual power: from altars to pulpits, from ritual mystery to </span><span class="c1">doctrinal certainty</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">.</span>

<span class="c7">Talal Asad&rsquo;s critique is instructive here: he argues that modern &ldquo;religion&rdquo; is constructed as a system of belief separated from everyday life and politics. The Reformation laid the groundwork for this by tying salvation to assent to creedal propositions (e.g. justification by faith) rather than to participation in the medieval cultic order. In other words, Protestantism helped produce the idea that religion is essentially </span><span class="c7 c8">belief and conscience</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">, not ritual practice. The Catholic sacramental universe, in which the spiritual was deeply woven into the fabric of communal life, largely collapsed into a more privatized inner piety.</span>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Myth, Belief, Organization, Ritual: A Comparative Framework</span> ===
<span class="c7">We may schematize the Reformation&rsquo;s effect on the four dimensions of religion: </span><span class="c1">myth</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(sacred narrative), </span><span class="c1">belief</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(doctrinal content), </span><span class="c1">organization</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(institutional structure), and </span><span class="c1">ritual</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">&nbsp;(symbolic practice).</span><ul class="c14 lst-kix_3rqluxr8qhwv-0 start"><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c7 c8">Myth.</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;Catholicism was rich in mythic narrative: creation stories, the lives of saints, martyr legends, the cosmic drama of Christ&rsquo;s death and sacrifice as &ldquo;salvation history.&rdquo; Protestants did not </span><span class="c1">invent</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;new myths, but they </span><span class="c7 c8">recast or expelled</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;the old ones. Biblical stories (e.g. the Exodus, Acts of the Apostles) were often read literally as &ldquo;holy history&rdquo; rather than allegory, but their interpretation became secularized (moral exemplars rather than mystical truths). Medieval myths like the intercession of saints, the cult of relics, or folk traditions (sprites, witches) were officially denounced as superstition. Nietzschean terms might say the Reformation &ldquo;killed the Father&rdquo; of myth, claiming progress required discarding the &ldquo;spontaneous religion&rdquo; of the people. Jean-Luc Nancy would note that this fits a monotheistic legacy: </span><span class="c7 c8">monotheism demythologizes</span><span class="c7">. As Nancy puts it, the Christian God &ldquo;atheizes himself&rdquo; by withdrawing from worldly story, ultimately signalling a world &ldquo;without God&rdquo;</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://politicaltheology.com/jean-luc-nancy/%23:~:text%3DA%2520world%2520without%2520God%2520is,all%2520is%2520dethroned%2520but%2520capital&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805553001&amp;usg=AOvVaw2NR-6cRWqUk4d1aMIIB223">politicaltheology.com</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">. Thus Protestantism pressed myth out of the church into individualized belief or history.<br></span>
</li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c7 c8">Belief.</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;Belief (doctrine) </span><span class="c1">rose</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;in prominence. The Reformers championed </span><span class="c1">sola scriptura</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(Scripture alone) and </span><span class="c1">sola fide</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(faith alone) &ndash; explicit propositional tenets about grace, election, and sacraments. Catechisms, confessions of faith, and theological debates proliferated. Intangible </span><span class="c7 c8">belief</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;became the litmus of religious identity. Each Protestant denomination codified its creed (Lutherans, Calvinists, Anglicans, etc.), so that </span><span class="c1">organized belief</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;now defined community. Ironically, this doctrinal focus was the new </span><span class="c1">mythic</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;core for believers: the myths had gone, but a rational narrative (from the Fall to the Last Judgment) took their place as a &ldquo;cognitive frame.&rdquo; Protestant preaching internalized biblical narrative into ethics (for example, Old Testament law became a moral story instead of a cosmic law imposed by a vicarious priesthood). The believer&rsquo;s experience became &ldquo;inner&rdquo; and </span><span class="c1">belief</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">-centered, satisfying Foucault&rsquo;s notion of the confessional &ndash; one now confessed faith and personal interpretation instead of penitent feeling. Rousseau and later secular thinkers would build on this, conceiving religion as &ldquo;voluntary&rdquo; creed anchored in conscience.<br></span>
</li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c7 c8">Organization.</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;Institutionally, Protestantism fragmented the monolithic medieval Church into </span><span class="c7 c8">many churches</span><span class="c7">. Each prince or city could set up its own church (often with a state-appointed bishop or consistory). The pre-Reformation Church&rsquo;s universal hierarchy was replaced by national or local structures. In some cases (England, Scandinavia), monarchs became heads of church. In others (Geneva, some German cities), civic councils or synods ruled. Layered beneath these were further splits into sects and free churches (Anabaptists, Baptists, etc.) that often rejected state ties. Weber noted that Protestantism spawned a sect&ndash;church cycle: </span><span class="c7 c8">sects</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(voluntary, schismatic groups with strict disciplines) and </span><span class="c7 c8">churches</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(state churches with formal membership) alternated, institutionalizing diversity. By contrast, medieval religion had been more geographically uniform, tied to local parishes but conceptually universal. In effect, Protestantism exported the logic of </span><span class="c1">institutional organization</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">&nbsp;to the modern world: religion became one sphere of life with its own bureaucracies, comparable to the new secular state. This was a key step toward the modern category &ldquo;organized religion&rdquo; &ndash; discrete societies governed by creeds and offices, distinct from (though often allied with) political power.<br></span>
</li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c7 c8">Ritual.</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;Protestant reformers drastically curtailed ritual. The medieval Mass, Marian devotions, fasts, pilgrimages, etc., were abolished or simplified. Only two sacraments remained (Baptism and the Lord&rsquo;s Supper), and these were stripped of Catholic magic. Ordinary believers now needed only a Bible and prayer, rather than rosaries or candles. Eucharistic ritual became brief and vernacular, preceded by sermons. As noted above, liturgy shifted toward &ldquo;clarity&rdquo; and community, suppressing mystery</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.catholicworldreport.com/2017/10/11/protestantism-in-the-catholic-church-the-emergence-of-a-shared-tradition/%23:~:text%3Dthat%2520have%2520influenced%2520the%2520way,of%2520Christ%2520over%2520these%2520elements&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805557231&amp;usg=AOvVaw3g94A1HfVKJK_WdOxapjXj">catholicworldreport.com</ref></span><span class="c7">. In sum, ritual and mythic performance </span><span class="c7 c8">lost their former centrality</span><span class="c7">. Protestants did not &ldquo;expel&rdquo; myth entirely (they still told Bible stories and sang psalms), but they relocated much that was once symbol into </span><span class="c1">moral narrative and ethical life</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">. Community solidarity relied more on schools, guilds, or nationhood than on religious fairs or processions. Sacramental grace, once a cosmic force, became an inner assurance.<br></span>
</li></ul><span class="c7">Altogether, Protestantism can be seen as favoring </span><span class="c1">belief and organization</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;over ritual and myth. It replaced a communal, embodied religion with a more disembodied, textually-grounded one. One might say it tried to secularize myth by making it historical (literal Bible accounts) or ethical (the world as stage for God&rsquo;s moral teaching), rather than leaving it as immanent sacral saga. Nancy&rsquo;s insight about capitalism is relevant: he contends that both monotheism and capitalism &ldquo;strip&rdquo; social life of narratives and values</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://politicaltheology.com/jean-luc-nancy/%23:~:text%3DFollowing%2520Marx%252C%2520Nancy%2520understands%2520that%252C,the%2520value%2520of%2520capital%2520alone&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805559221&amp;usg=AOvVaw2MP2Q3DoOmMylPXqXgHeH_">politicaltheology.com</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">. Protestantism&rsquo;s rational morality and market-friendly individualism anticipated that process, leaving religion itself as one value-sphere (of belief) among others.</span>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Long-Term Effects: Privatized Belief and the Making of Secular Religion</span> ===
<span class="c7">The structural shift initiated by Protestant reform </span><span class="c7 c8">paved the way for the modern concept of religion</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;as chiefly private belief. In the Protestant mold, religion became what one </span><span class="c1">believes</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;&ndash; doctrines on paper &ndash; rather than what one </span><span class="c1">does</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;in ritual. This idea underlies our contemporary categories: &ldquo;organized religion,&rdquo; &ldquo;belief system,&rdquo; &ldquo;secular faith.&rdquo; As one recent scholar notes, the very notions of &ldquo;religion&rdquo; and &ldquo;secularity&rdquo; in today&rsquo;s liberal West are modeled on Enlightenment Protestant assumptions</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41682-023-00156-1%23:~:text%3DAs%2520I%25C2%25A0will%2520argue%2520in%2520the,both%2520religion%2520and%2520secularity%2520are&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805561276&amp;usg=AOvVaw1PvZ6KNYSNdtzA1mhQ7UWx">link.springer.com</ref></span><span class="c7">. He writes: </span><span class="c1">&ldquo;When the modern concept of religion took shape, it was in the context of Enlightenment Protestantism, which became the model for religion as such.&rdquo;</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41682-023-00156-1%23:~:text%3DAs%2520I%25C2%25A0will%2520argue%2520in%2520the,both%2520religion%2520and%2520secularity%2520are&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805561907&amp;usg=AOvVaw0wpxQwxQrWlRl0BbkL6bn9">link.springer.com</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">. In other words, to be &ldquo;religious&rdquo; came to mean having interior convictions and private conscience &ndash; exactly the Reformation&rsquo;s emphasis.</span>

<span class="c13 c7 c20">This shift had key implications:</span><ul class="c14 lst-kix_flcpi6oo5tre-0 start"><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c7 c8">Privatization of Belief.</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">&nbsp;Protestant theology broke religion into personal faith. Each individual was encouraged to read the Bible and judge doctrine by conscience. The idea of a secular state could rest on the notion that religion is an optional, individual loyalty (as Jefferson and Madison later argued), not a corporate obligation. Indeed, the language of &ldquo;religious liberty&rdquo; &ndash; freedom of opinion in matters of faith &ndash; assumes religion is about inner assent. Talal Asad and others observe that modern human rights discourse redefines religion as &ldquo;creedal&rdquo; and &ldquo;deeply held belief.&rdquo; This could hardly have emerged without Protestant influence; Catholics and Orthodox long defined religion in communal, sacramental terms (e.g. participation in the church, not mere belief).<br></span>
</li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c7 c8">Separation of Church and State.</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">&nbsp;Confessional Europe in 1650 was still a world of established churches. But the Reformation&rsquo;s legacy is a slow shift toward disestablishment. The wars of religion taught that enforcing uniform ritual breeds unrest; thinkers like Locke (a Puritan) argued for toleration precisely because faith was seen as inward. By the 19th century, many states claimed neutrality toward church beliefs, creating a public/private divide. This &ldquo;secular&rdquo; political order assumes religion is just one sector. It was imaginable because reformers had first relegated rites to the domestic sphere and invoked an autonomous conscience.<br></span>
</li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c7 c8">Organized Religion as Category.</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;The pluralism of Protestant sects itself established the norm of &ldquo;organized religion&rdquo; versus beliefs. Scholars of religion note that Protestant denominationalism provided the template for later religious identity groups everywhere. Even today, when sociologists study Buddhism or Islam, they often implicitly assume &ldquo;believers&rdquo; whose lives revolve around theology and moral commitments, a model inherited from Christianity. Nancy&rsquo;s and Taylor&rsquo;s work both remind us that our conceptual universe (religion, secularity, belief) emerged from a distinctly Western, Protestant-infused history</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41682-023-00156-1%23:~:text%3DAs%2520I%25C2%25A0will%2520argue%2520in%2520the,both%2520religion%2520and%2520secularity%2520are&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805566779&amp;usg=AOvVaw05l_7MPEtsdhEIwu0MAC4Y">link.springer.com</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://politicaltheology.com/jean-luc-nancy/%23:~:text%3DA%2520world%2520without%2520God%2520is,all%2520is%2520dethroned%2520but%2520capital&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805567083&amp;usg=AOvVaw0yW-u-aSq6CGOD3IrnImxr">politicaltheology.com</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">.<br></span>
</li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c7 c8">Secular Categories.</span><span class="c13 c7 c20">&nbsp;Finally, Protestant reforms seeded secular ideas. By exiling myth and ritual from public life, Protestant culture helped carve out a separate realm for &ldquo;the world.&rdquo; Capital accumulation and statecraft (themselves fostered by Protestant ethics) became &ldquo;secular&rdquo; pursuits, distinct from &ldquo;religious&rdquo; redemption. Foucault&rsquo;s notion of governmentality &ndash; power over life &ndash; finds an ironic foreshadowing in the Reformation: Luther&rsquo;s teaching that princes govern God&rsquo;s people, and Calvin&rsquo;s theocratic city planning, were early forms of managing populations. The long-term result is a worldview where belief systems (like Christianity) coexist with other ideologies, none absolute.<br></span>
</li></ul><span class="c7">In sum, the Protestant Reformation initiated a </span><span class="c7 c8">genealogy of modern religion</span><span class="c7">. By substituting inward faith for outward magic, and doctrine for sacrament, it laid the groundwork for the very idea of religion as we know it today &ndash; a private belief system organized into churches, separate from the secular state and stripped of the mythic depth that once animated medieval life</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3Dhomoge%2502neous%2520event,absolutely%2520decisive%2520difference%2520from%2520Catholicism&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805569223&amp;usg=AOvVaw3i2JEY4ljVYVvsFshF1N6u">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s41682-023-00156-1%23:~:text%3DAs%2520I%25C2%25A0will%2520argue%2520in%2520the,both%2520religion%2520and%2520secularity%2520are&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805569463&amp;usg=AOvVaw0hmarPVtWBOs3avA9HPM8O">link.springer.com</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">.</span>

<span class="c7 c8">Sources:</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;This analysis draws on historical and social-scientific scholarship. For economics, see Cantoni </span><span class="c1">et al.</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(2017) on the redistribution of church wealth</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3DUsing%2520novel%2520microdata%252C%2520we%2520document,This%2520transfer%2520of%2520resources%2520had&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805569937&amp;usg=AOvVaw3hVFAQpNZEaXvMdDk8zMTx">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.nber.org/papers/w23934%23:~:text%3Dfor%2520public%2520sector%2520jobs%252C%2520rather,the%2520secularization%2520of%2520the%2520West&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805570098&amp;usg=AOvVaw1n6yTHVxx7jeCn861onTp7">nber.org</ref></span><span class="c7">&nbsp;and Ekelund </span><span class="c1">et al.</span><span class="c7">&nbsp;(2002) on Weber and capitalist motives</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3Dhomoge%2502neous%2520event,absolutely%2520decisive%2520difference%2520from%2520Catholicism&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805570407&amp;usg=AOvVaw2l2EVnVFMhAAbbjD92VjmF">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3D%25E2%2580%25A2,control%2520of%2520the%2520individual%2520which&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805570583&amp;usg=AOvVaw2W2aEnEDGhJIF5z_H9ZLY8">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c7">. For ritual and iconoclasm, see D&#382;alto (2024) on iconophobiadiva-portal.org and contemporary surveys of liturgy</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.catholicworldreport.com/2017/10/11/protestantism-in-the-catholic-church-the-emergence-of-a-shared-tradition/%23:~:text%3Dthat%2520have%2520influenced%2520the%2520way,of%2520Christ%2520over%2520these%2520elements&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805570922&amp;usg=AOvVaw2Ht0Kmr54PbnBSUZVjguUd">catholicworldreport.com</ref></span><span class="c7">. On sectarian utopias, see the M&uuml;nster Anabaptist chronicles</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://gameo.org/index.php?title%3DM%25C3%25BCnster_Anabaptists%23:~:text%3Dbeen%2520sent%2520to%2520M%25C3%25BCnster%2520by,Others%2520were&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805571154&amp;usg=AOvVaw2B0TTYroQR671vaLB9zHOi">gameo.org</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://gameo.org/index.php?title%3DM%25C3%25BCnster_Anabaptists%23:~:text%3DMeanwhile%252C%2520Bishop%2520Franz%2520of%2520Waldeck%252C,gave%2520them%2520authority%2520in%2520the&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805571313&amp;usg=AOvVaw1KLX4iQMorjkwpg_K-ahHw">gameo.org</ref></span><span class="c7">. On doctrinal transformation and the Protestant </span><span class="c7 c8">sacramental collapse</span><span class="c7">, see Weber&rsquo;s account</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://web.stanford.edu/~avner/Greif_228_2005/Ekelund%2520et%2520al%25202002%2520JPE%2520Reformation.pdf%23:~:text%3Dhomoge%2502neous%2520event,absolutely%2520decisive%2520difference%2520from%2520Catholicism&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805571633&amp;usg=AOvVaw1pJC-7y0ZAXZX16fsCTOJB">web.stanford.edu</ref></span><span class="c7">&nbsp;and Luther&rsquo;s own </span><span class="c1">Freedom of a Christian</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://ccel.org/ccel/luther/christianliberty/christianliberty.iii.html%23:~:text%3Dspiritual%2520liberty%2520and%2520servitude%253A%25E2%2580%2594&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805571870&amp;usg=AOvVaw3lV1y1dy0Ka6wf7xvP9YXK">ccel.org</ref></span><span class="c7">. On myth and modern religion, we employ post-structuralist insights: Nancy&rsquo;s deconstruction of Christian modernity</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://politicaltheology.com/jean-luc-nancy/%23:~:text%3DA%2520world%2520without%2520God%2520is,all%2520is%2520dethroned%2520but%2520capital&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805572162&amp;usg=AOvVaw1C1DT401d09xg7P9PGVytl">politicaltheology.com</ref></span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://politicaltheology.com/jean-luc-nancy/%23:~:text%3DFollowing%2520Marx%252C%2520Nancy%2520understands%2520that%252C,the%2520value%2520of%2520capital%2520alone&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805572321&amp;usg=AOvVaw1VdfwnTOmr9Xo7NDlw7gDQ">politicaltheology.com</ref></span><span class="c7">&nbsp;and Taylor&rsquo;s narrative of secularization</span><span class="c9 c17"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://tif.ssrc.org/2007/10/19/secularism-of-a-new-kind/%23:~:text%3DTaylor%2520argues%2520that%2520the%2520Reformation%25E2%2580%2594with,with%2520its%2520emphasis%2520on%2520progress&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805572542&amp;usg=AOvVaw3oht2TNKt3NNxYQw1b5Caa">tif.ssrc.org</ref></span><span class="c13 c7 c20">. Together, these sources substantiate how Protestantism restructured Western religiosity &ndash; a shift from communal mythic ritual to individualized belief and doctrinal order.</span>

==== <span class="c7 c8">1&#8239;&#8239;Redefining &ldquo;faith&rdquo; as an </span><span class="c1 c8">inner</span><span class="c13 c7 c8">&nbsp;state</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Medieval Christianity had understood </span><span class="c6">fides</span><span>&nbsp;as an </span><span class="c8">embodied habitus</span><span>&mdash;a virtue formed by charity (</span><span class="c6">fides formata caritate</span><span>) and enacted through sacrament and community.&#8239;Aquinas: &ldquo;faith is </span><span class="c6">formed</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;by charity; charity makes faith perfect.&rdquo;</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c3">Early reformers reversed the vector.</span></p><ul class="c14 lst-kix_e5l8xxwnuuh3-0 start"><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Martin&#8239;Luther</span><span>&nbsp;called faith &ldquo;</span><span class="c6">a living, daring confidence in God&rsquo;s grace, so sure and certain that a man could stake his life on it a thousand times</span><span>.&rdquo;<br> </span><span class="c22 c20 c6">The &ldquo;confidence&rdquo; happens in the conscience; ritual can only preach or symbolize it.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">John&#8239;Calvin</span><span>&nbsp;tightened the definition: &ldquo;</span><span class="c6">Faith is a firm and certain knowledge of God&rsquo;s favor toward us, founded upon the truth of the freely given promise in Christ.</span><span class="c3">&rdquo;<br></span></li></ul><p class="c0"><span>In both cases, </span><span class="c8">knowledge&#8209;of&#8209;grace displaces participation&#8209;in&#8209;grace</span><span>. Where Aquinas located faith in a sacramental ecology, Luther and Calvin locate it </span><span class="c8">inside the judging subject</span><span>&mdash;a decisive step toward the </span><span class="c6">buffered self</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;that Charles&#8239;Taylor sees as the hallmark of secularity .</span></p><hr><p class="c0 c10"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">2&#8239;&#8239;Sola&#8239;fide and the birth of Protestant anxiety</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Because salvation now rests on an invisible disposition, believers had to </span><span class="c8">audit their own interior</span><span>. Luther&rsquo;s vocabulary of </span><span class="c6">Anfechtung</span><span>&nbsp;(assaults of doubt) captures the mood: the Word &ldquo;</span><span class="c6">teaches you &hellip; to experience how right, how true, how sweet &hellip; God&rsquo;s Word is</span><span class="c3">&rdquo; only through struggle and anxiety .</span></p><p class="c0"><span>By the 17th&#8239;c. Puritans were urged to keep </span><span class="c8">spiritual &ldquo;registers&rdquo;</span><span class="c3">&mdash;journals in which daily feelings were interrogated for evidence of grace:</span></p><p class="c0 c26"><span>&ldquo;Self&#8209;examination is the setting up a court in conscience and </span><span class="c6">keeping a register there</span><span class="c3">, that by strict scrutiny a man may know how things stand between God and his own soul.&rdquo; (Thomas&#8239;Watson)</span></p><p class="c0"><span>The result, as historian Stannard notes, was an </span><span class="c6">&ldquo;intense and unremitting fear of death&rdquo;</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;produced by God&rsquo;s inscrutable choice .</span></p><hr><p class="c0 c10"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">3&#8239;&#8239;Predestination and the double bind</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Calvinist predestination </span><span class="c8">intensified the loop</span><span>: inward assurance is both </span><span class="c6">sign</span><span>&nbsp;of election and something no act of will can secure. Diaries, sermons, and tracts therefore teach believers to read every tremor of the heart as possible evidence&mdash;while warning that self&#8209;deception is omnipresent. John&#8239;Bunyan&rsquo;s </span><span class="c6">Grace Abounding</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;swings between terror and relief, memorializing each doubt so that it can serve as later proof of deliverance.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>The Calvinist must therefore </span><span class="c8">believe sincerely</span><span>&nbsp;</span><span class="c6">and</span><span>&nbsp;</span><span class="c8">perform belief strategically</span><span>&mdash;a proto&#8209;modern </span><span class="c6">doublethink</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;in which the self polices itself for the right affect.</span></p><hr><p class="c0 c10"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">4&#8239;&#8239;From confessional interior to self&#8209;surveillance</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span class="c3">Michel&#8239;Foucault supplies the genealogy:</span></p><ul class="c14 lst-kix_4zm5unro13x-0 start"><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span>&ldquo;</span><span class="c6">He who is subjected to a field of visibility &hellip; inscribes in himself the power relation &hellip; he becomes the principle of his own subjection.</span><span class="c3">&rdquo;<br></span></li></ul><p class="c0"><span>The Protestant sermon replaces the Catholic confessional booth; but the logic is identical: the believer internalizes the gaze and turns it on the self </span><span class="c8">continuously</span><span>. Louis&#8239;Althusser&rsquo;s axiom&mdash;&ldquo;</span><span class="c6">there is no ideology except by the subject and for the subject</span><span>&rdquo; &mdash;describes precisely this transition: faith becomes an </span><span class="c8">ideological interpellation</span><span>&nbsp;that calls &ldquo;</span><span class="c6">You!</span><span class="c3">&rdquo; and is answered in an inward voice.</span></p><hr><p class="c0 c10"></p>

==== <span class="c7 c8">5&#8239;&#8239;Catholic &amp; Orthodox alternatives: faith as </span><span class="c1 c28 c8">communion</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Catholic theology keeps faith entwined with sacrament: it is perfected by charity (</span><span class="c6">habitus</span><span class="c3">) and enacted corporeally in Eucharist, pilgrimage, penance. Eastern Orthodoxy radicalizes this relational ontology.&#8239;John&#8239;Zizioulas:</span></p><p class="c0 c26"><span>&ldquo;</span><span class="c6">All communion must involve otherness as a primary and constitutive ingredient &hellip; freedom is part of the notion of being.</span><span class="c3">&rdquo;</span></p><p class="c0"><span>Here </span><span class="c8">faith = shared liturgy</span><span class="c3">, not private certitude. The ecclesial body, not the introspective conscience, mediates salvation&mdash;short&#8209;circuiting the solitary anxiety that haunted Protestants.</span></p><hr><p class="c0 c10"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">6&#8239;&#8239;Philosophers of the Protestant interior</span> ====
<table class="c33"><tr class="c29"><td class="c31" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c27"><span class="c8">Thinker</span></p></td><td class="c24" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c27"><span class="c8">Echo of Protestant turn</span></p></td></tr><tr class="c15"><td class="c31" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c0"><span class="c8">S&oslash;ren&#8239;Kierkegaard</span><span>&nbsp;&ndash; &ldquo;</span><span class="c6">Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.</span><span class="c3">&rdquo;</span></p></td><td class="c24" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c0"><span class="c3">Heightens the subjective tension: freedom and dread are inseparable once faith is internal decision.</span></p></td></tr><tr class="c15"><td class="c31" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Ludwig&#8239;Wittgenstein</span><span>&nbsp;&ndash; &ldquo;</span><span class="c6">The meaning of a word is its use.</span><span class="c3">&rdquo;</span></p></td><td class="c24" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c0"><span class="c3">Shifts truth from inner assent to public practice&mdash;an implicit critique of faith-as-proposition.</span></p></td></tr><tr class="c15"><td class="c31" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Max&#8239;Weber</span><span>&nbsp;&ndash; &ldquo;</span><span class="c6">The light cloak of piety became an iron cage.</span><span>&rdquo;</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/weber/protestant-ethic/ch05.htm?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805581051&amp;usg=AOvVaw1ZZL6HUJ7HIw5vP8OHA-5F">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.marxists.org/reference/archive/weber/protestant-ethic/ch05.htm?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805581314&amp;usg=AOvVaw2Q85r4t4hDh5TntJj7PPmB">Marxists Internet Archive</ref></span></p></td><td class="c24" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c0"><span class="c3">Diagnoses how Protestant self&#8209;discipline solidifies into impersonal rationalized structures.</span></p></td></tr><tr class="c15"><td class="c31" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Charles&#8239;Taylor</span><span>&nbsp;&ndash; Reformation births the &ldquo;</span><span class="c6">buffered self</span><span class="c3">,&rdquo; protected from spirits yet tasked with self&#8209;management.</span></p></td><td class="c24" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c0 c10"><span class="c3"></span></p></td></tr><tr class="c15"><td class="c31" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Michel&#8239;Foucault</span><span>&nbsp;&ndash; under neoliberalism the worker &ldquo;</span><span class="c6">appears as a sort of enterprise for himself</span><span class="c3">.&rdquo;</span></p></td><td class="c24" colspan="1" rowspan="1"><p class="c0"><span class="c3">The Protestant audit of conscience mutates into market&#8209;style audit of the self.</span></p></td></tr></table><hr><p class="c0 c10"></p>

==== <span class="c7 c8 c13">7&#8239;&#8239;From anxious believer to neoliberal subject</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Foucault&rsquo;s Chicago&#8209;school lecture shows the arc: once the soul is taught to ask &ldquo;Do I truly believe?&rdquo; it can just as well ask &ldquo;Am&#8239;I maximising my human capital?&rdquo; Neoliberal governmentality recodes conscience as </span><span class="c8">permanent economic self&#8209;assessment</span><span class="c3">&mdash;&ldquo;entrepreneurs of themselves&rdquo; rather than pilgrims toward grace.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c3">The earlier Protestant schema supplied:</span></p><ol class="c14 lst-kix_qng9cnb2t3oc-0 start" start="1"><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Interior criterion</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;(faith&#8239;&rarr;&#8239;performance metrics)<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Continuous self&#8209;examination</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;(spiritual journal&#8239;&rarr;&#8239;data dashboard)<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Anxiety as proof of sincerity</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;(Anfechtung&#8239;&rarr;&#8239;&ldquo;hustle culture&rdquo;)<br></span></li></ol><hr><p class="c0 c10"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">8&#8239;&#8239;Conclusion</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>The Reformation&rsquo;s redefinition of faith&mdash;</span><span class="c6">from sacramental habitus to psychological state</span><span>&mdash;generated a new form of </span><span class="c8">self&#8209;relating subjectivity</span><span>. Its legacy runs from Puritan diaries to the </span><span class="c8">modern &ldquo;entrepreneur of the self.&rdquo;</span><span>&nbsp;Understanding this arc is crucial for any critique of contemporary religiosity (including neo&#8209;pagan revivals): the field in which new myths are planted has already been ploughed by Protestant interiorization, anxiety, and the ideological demand to </span><span class="c6">mean what we perform while performing what we must mean</span><span class="c3">.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c20 c6 c22">(For fuller development see Weber 1905; Foucault 1979; Taylor 2007; Asad 1993; Cavanaugh 2008.)</span></p><p class="c0 c10"><span class="c3"></span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Evangelicalism as Late&#8209;Capitalist </span><span class="c8 c6">Reterritorialization<br></span><span>&nbsp;</span><span class="c22 c20 c6">(A Marxist&ndash;Deleuzian reading of how U&#8239;S&#8209;style evangelicalism stabilizes the neoliberal order while masking its own contradictions)</span></p><hr>

=== Deleuze stuff ===
<span class="c3"></span>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">1&#8239;&#8239;From &ldquo;decoding&rdquo; to brute domination</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Deleuze &amp;&#8239;Guattari describe capitalism as the first social machine that &ldquo;constitutes itself on the failure of all pre&#8209;existent codes,&rdquo; liberating every flow only to recapture it in new axioms of control</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://deleuzelectures.blogspot.com/2007/02/capitalism-flows-decoding-of-flows.html?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805586326&amp;usg=AOvVaw3GoptB5YjgBqfQ4IdKEEh7">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://deleuzelectures.blogspot.com/2007/02/capitalism-flows-decoding-of-flows.html?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805586558&amp;usg=AOvVaw0GMdb3BBtBVsbNRZ5J8gHh">Lectures by Gilles Deleuze</ref></span><span>. Mainline Protestantism carried out an early wave of this </span><span class="c8">decoding</span><span>&mdash;dissolving Catholic liturgies into interior belief (your previous chapter). Contemporary U&#8239;S. evangelicalism represents the </span><span class="c6">next</span><span>&nbsp;stage: having eaten away even its own Reformation foundations (confession, creeds, catechesis), it re&#8209;imposes </span><span class="c8">simplified commands</span><span>&mdash;&ldquo;believe, submit, consume&rdquo;&mdash;as what Deleuze calls </span><span class="c6">pure domination</span><span class="c3">, a yassified tradition that survives precisely because of its austerity.</span></p><p class="c0 c26"><span>&ldquo;Christianity taught us to see the eye of the lord looking down upon us&hellip; Their function is to tame, and the result is the fabrication of docile and obedient subjects.&rdquo; &mdash;</span><span class="c6">Anti&#8209;Oedipus</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.goodreads.com/work/quotes/113899-capitalisme-et-schizophr-nie-1-l-anti--dipe?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805587528&amp;usg=AOvVaw1WF5ZXe_HlPuLRI4gzUlVA">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.goodreads.com/work/quotes/113899-capitalisme-et-schizophr-nie-1-l-anti--dipe?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805587714&amp;usg=AOvVaw04-NdSK77dZq5IA7sCA3rm">Goodreads</ref></span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">2&#8239;&#8239;The prosperity gospel &amp; spiritualized neoliberalism</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Kathryn&#8239;Lofton argues that Oprah Winfrey&rsquo;s media empire is </span><span class="c8">&ldquo;religion for an age in which markets make custom, consumption is the universal aspect, and celebrities are ostensible gods.&rdquo;</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://buddhiststudies.stanford.edu/events/kathryn-lofton-spiritual-capitalism-prosperity-gospel-oprah-winfrey?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805588320&amp;usg=AOvVaw33tX1MaeYVM2xSqHRGy7al">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://buddhiststudies.stanford.edu/events/kathryn-lofton-spiritual-capitalism-prosperity-gospel-oprah-winfrey?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805588504&amp;usg=AOvVaw1gf1nI96poC0wosNOTe-dU">Ho Center for Buddhist Studies</ref></span><span>&nbsp;Prosperity&#8209;gospel megachurches extend this &ldquo;spiritual capitalism&rdquo; to the working poor: salvation is re&#8209;coded as personal brand management (&ldquo;live your best life now&rdquo;), while structural exploitation is renamed </span><span class="c6">blessing</span><span>. The result meshes smoothly with neoliberal responsibilization: </span><span class="c6">if you&rsquo;re broke, tithe harder.</span><span>&nbsp;An African megachurch study finds worship music itself operates as a </span><span class="c8">&ldquo;neoliberal apparatus&rdquo;</span><span>&nbsp;that trains believers to oscillate between prayer and product</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.academia.edu/39948074/Prayer_Product_Duality_Megachurch_Worship_Music_as_Neoliberal_Apparatus?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805589240&amp;usg=AOvVaw1_OkQpqyU34iNOcWkIN1AY">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.academia.edu/39948074/Prayer_Product_Duality_Megachurch_Worship_Music_as_Neoliberal_Apparatus?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805589430&amp;usg=AOvVaw0jkUnqah4V6nqGMPuqOeTG">Academia</ref></span><span class="c3">.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">3&#8239;&#8239;Contemporary worship as commodity&#8209;capture</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>A 2022 study shows five megachurch labels&mdash;Hillsong, Bethel, Elevation, Passion, Maverick City&mdash;now </span><span class="c8">dominate the worship charts</span><span>, creating a closed market for affective religious goods</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://apnews.com/article/worship-music-hit-makers-bethel-hillsong-elevation-passion-2982ab331782af96cfcc67a974793961?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805590174&amp;usg=AOvVaw2kuzldN5H5DIqNM3oWxOpb">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://apnews.com/article/worship-music-hit-makers-bethel-hillsong-elevation-passion-2982ab331782af96cfcc67a974793961?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805590355&amp;usg=AOvVaw2mUWvdarI0nQVPyf9kTqPo">AP News</ref></span><span>. Hillsong&rsquo;s own researchers call this the evolution from </span><span class="c6">congregation</span><span>&nbsp;to </span><span class="c8">global brand</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/301895156_The_Evolution_of_Hillsong_Music_From_Australian_Pentecostal_congregation_into_Global_Brand?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805590723&amp;usg=AOvVaw3-cKsVqmPjrGJTAoVRMMYa">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/301895156_The_Evolution_of_Hillsong_Music_From_Australian_Pentecostal_congregation_into_Global_Brand?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805590924&amp;usg=AOvVaw3KKmsfDQIezZdSg2Z0xtQy">ResearchGate</ref></span><span>. The music&rsquo;s four&#8209;chord anthems supply what Marx called </span><span class="c6">commodity fetishism</span><span>: believers consume the </span><span class="c6">sound</span><span>&nbsp;of transcendence while remaining tied to screens, smoke machines, and point&#8209;of&#8209;sale tithing apps. Thus evangelicalism does not merely bless capitalism; it </span><span class="c8">functions as capitalism&rsquo;s liturgy</span><span class="c3">.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">4&#8239;&#8239;Patriarchy as last&#8209;ditch reterritorialization</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Kristin&#8239;Kobes&#8239;Du&#8239;Mez shows how white evangelical culture &ldquo;glorifies the aggressive, patriarchal idea of manhood&rdquo; in order to stabilize the movement after the feminist and civil&#8209;rights upheavals of the 1960s</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://kristindumez.com/books/jesus-and-john-wayne/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805592270&amp;usg=AOvVaw0c9U-qWJnzbd5xpwzlF2Y1">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://kristindumez.com/books/jesus-and-john-wayne/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805592501&amp;usg=AOvVaw1plDlpwQuaBhIeArHdYIhP">Kristin Kobes Du Mez</ref></span><span class="c3">. Purity&#8209;culture literature channels that patriarchy into biopolitical surveillance of girls&rsquo; bodies:</span></p><p class="c0 c26"><span>&ldquo;At the core of purity culture is patriarchy and the message that, compared to men, women don&rsquo;t matter all that much.&rdquo;</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://reformedjournal.com/2018/10/06/evangelicalism-purity-culture-and-patriarchy/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805593178&amp;usg=AOvVaw21M_8_HIRsWYgr1SUm3Snv">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://reformedjournal.com/2018/10/06/evangelicalism-purity-culture-and-patriarchy/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805593403&amp;usg=AOvVaw1B53GVElwUModAqvq5_4XT">Reformed Journal</ref></span></p><p class="c0"><span>Such teaching no longer grants men genuine provider status (Fordist wages are gone) yet insists women &ldquo;submit&rdquo; so the nuclear family can still service consumer debt and unpaid care work. Marx would call this an ideological </span><span class="c8">super&#8209;structure</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;masking the unpaid reproductive labor that capitalism requires.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">5&#8239;&#8239;Homophobia, transphobia, and the policing of decoded subjects</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Sexual minorities expose the bare fact that contemporary worship has </span><span class="c6">no</span><span>&nbsp;thick theology of embodiment&mdash;only slogans about &ldquo;male headship.&rdquo; Hence queer existence is experienced by the movement as a threat to its already thinned code. Anthea&#8239;Butler bluntly notes that racism sits &ldquo;at the core of conservative evangelical activism and power&rdquo;</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://uncpress.org/book/9781469661179/white-evangelical-racism/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805595273&amp;usg=AOvVaw0kV-KwrslXUO_jdbh86h8t">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://uncpress.org/book/9781469661179/white-evangelical-racism/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805595536&amp;usg=AOvVaw1y5ka6SjyIuEoQeFTcS8Zl">University of North Carolina Press</ref></span><span>; the same holds for heteronormativity. Both function as </span><span class="c8">boundary&#8209;drawing devices</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;that harden group identity even as economic policies (gig work, medical debt) erode everyday stability.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">6&#8239;&#8239;Exceptions and counter&#8209;flows</span> ====
<ul class="c14 lst-kix_s1h6y6a2jhoz-0 start"><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Black evangelicals.</span><span>&nbsp;Black churches often carry </span><span class="c6">evangelical</span><span>&nbsp;theology but graft it onto liberationist praxis: James&#8239;Cone&rsquo;s dictum that God is &ldquo;unreservedly identified with the oppressed&rdquo; remains influential</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9930479/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805596659&amp;usg=AOvVaw1hLR6wBulO3p9sbuldEtvA">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9930479/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805596796&amp;usg=AOvVaw1Rw2IUq3vGP5S13Du4hnoo">PMC</ref></span><span>. Economic&#8209;justice coalitions led by Black evangelicals show flashes of </span><span class="c8">class consciousness</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;even while retaining conservative sexual ethics.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Midwestern cooperatives &amp; &ldquo;new evangelicals.&rdquo;</span><span>&nbsp;Historians trace strands of populist anti&#8209;bank, pro&#8209;labor activism within small&#8209;town Midwestern churches, a reminder that evangelical </span><span class="c6">forms</span><span>&nbsp;can host divergent </span><span class="c6">contents</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://marciapally.com/the-theology-of-economic-justice-creation-care-new-evangelicals/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805597517&amp;usg=AOvVaw2darXC8tPHS6eeT4UU2cR1">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://marciapally.com/the-theology-of-economic-justice-creation-care-new-evangelicals/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805597682&amp;usg=AOvVaw3lrM9LPgHSNxV1TAotnY5t">Marcia Pally</ref></span><span class="c3">. These counter&#8209;flows prove that the movement is not monolithic but rather a contested field of deterritorialized affects.<br></span></li></ul><hr><p class="c2"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">7&#8239;&#8239;Comparative detour: &ldquo;Islamic Calvinism&rdquo; in Turkey</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>A 2005 European Stability Initiative report coined </span><span class="c8">&ldquo;Islamic Calvinism&rdquo;</span><span>&nbsp;for Anatolian entrepreneurs who wed free&#8209;market discipline to Islamic piety; Turkish analysts show this fusion arose as neoliberal globalization incentivized &ldquo;probusiness values&rdquo; and used religion to neutralize the left</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://islampolthoughtinturkey.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/Publication-Available.pdf?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805598536&amp;usg=AOvVaw3_sd6gM9GMKRYhNPVJbL3F">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://islampolthoughtinturkey.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/10/Publication-Available.pdf?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805598725&amp;usg=AOvVaw3hQegA2hHy7-GrBQXTjLK3">islampolthoughtinturkey.com</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/292913252_Does_economic_history_repeat_itself_Religion_work_ethic_and_economic_growth_in_modern_Turkey?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805598907&amp;usg=AOvVaw2whTscX_aeP4FKrpWQAStA">ResearchGate</ref></span><span>. Saudi Wahhabism remains over&#8209;coded and petro&#8209;state funded; Erdo&#287;an&#8209;era Turkish Islam, by contrast, resembles U&#8239;S. evangelicalism&rsquo;s </span><span class="c8">lean, motivational style</span><span class="c3">, making it an ideal vector for capitalist modernization.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">8&#8239;&#8239;The Cold&#8209;War genealogy: from segregation academies to global &ldquo;special ops&rdquo;</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>The religious&#8209;right coalition that crystallized in the 1970s redirected segregationist anger into a pro&#8209;life crusade, providing an anti&#8209;communist moral front. </span><span class="c6">Special&#8209;ops</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;organizations amplify this project:</span></p><ul class="c14 lst-kix_hhn0wdw65736-0 start"><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Opus&#8239;Dei</span><span>&nbsp;operated transnational anti&#8209;communist networks and helped spread neoliberal Catholic politics</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://aha.confex.com/aha/2013/webprogram/Paper12337.html?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805600042&amp;usg=AOvVaw2yj6oNkTXaFqPdQL-aqhzY">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://aha.confex.com/aha/2013/webprogram/Paper12337.html?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805600210&amp;usg=AOvVaw1t8xCBogVuLFrLHqeRXfHX">AHA Conference Management</ref></span><span class="c3">.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span>The </span><span class="c8">Unification Church</span><span>&nbsp;funded the World League for Freedom and Democracy and other anti&#8209;Soviet projects, and still shifts its vast assets into U&#8239;S. lobbying</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_Church_and_politics?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805600614&amp;usg=AOvVaw36OvuxlyAyyvbyUYSReJdl">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_Church_and_politics?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805600764&amp;usg=AOvVaw0jyaMvqqvBL3VYqt8z430O">Wikipedia</ref></span><span
