class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://time.com/6961050/unification-church-ffwp-moonies-us-election/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805600951&amp;usg=AOvVaw3wIaMnbMm9lY8ohFB5Kl-n">Time</ref></span><span class="c3">.<br></span></li></ul><p class="c0"><span class="c3">Both groups model how religious minimalism plus media spectacle can serve geopolitical capitalism beyond Protestant borders.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">9&#8239;&#8239;Mechanisms of consent: self&#8209;surveillance and entrepreneurial piety</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Foucault&rsquo;s &ldquo;technologies of the self&rdquo; explain why the evangelical believer is an ideal neoliberal citizen: she </span><span class="c8">audits her soul</span><span>&nbsp;(quiet&#8209;time apps, accountability groups) the way a gig worker audits brand metrics</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governmentality?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805601830&amp;usg=AOvVaw24MsDl8VTDALDsSEVzKR78">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governmentality?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805601964&amp;usg=AOvVaw3ofc8F80AHk2eS-GrXxLDi">Wikipedia</ref></span><span>. A recent Kenyan essay observes that the state welcomes church evangelists because they &ldquo;co&#8209;opt the proletariat who would object to neoliberal policies&rdquo;</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.theelephant.info/opinion/2023/02/24/state-evangelism-in-a-neoliberal-economy/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805602276&amp;usg=AOvVaw0K_Nam1q33jX3ORLRojmk7">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.theelephant.info/opinion/2023/02/24/state-evangelism-in-a-neoliberal-economy/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805602479&amp;usg=AOvVaw26By9sKvF_DHUN_wLKe3YQ">theelephant.info</ref></span><span>. In Althusser&rsquo;s terms, the worship set &ldquo;interpellates&rdquo; the subject&mdash;</span><span class="c6">You there, lifting your hands, you are free!</span><span class="c3">&mdash;while siphoning surplus value upward through offerings and media subscriptions.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

==== <span class="c7 c8">10&#8239;&#8239;Conclusion: evangelicalism as </span><span class="c1 c8 c28">reterritorialization of decoded flows</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Evangelicalism stabilizes late&#8209;capitalist crisis by </span><span class="c8">simplifying belief, aesthetic, and social order</span><span>&nbsp;to the bare minimum required for continued extraction. Its megachurch soundscape and purity rules are not nostalgic returns to tradition; they are the </span><span class="c6">cheap plastic scaffolding</span><span>&nbsp;erected after decades of neoliberal demolition. Yet counter&#8209;flows&mdash;from Black liberationist preaching to Anatolian businessmen re&#8209;imagining Islamic piety&mdash;show that decoded desire can still exceed the axioms. As Deleuze &amp;&#8239;Guattari warn, the very flows that capitalism unleashes may ultimately &ldquo;destroy the socius&rdquo; it tries to save</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.reddit.com/r/Deleuze/comments/1in80s0/what_do_you_make_of_the_famous_accelerate_the/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805603994&amp;usg=AOvVaw2gbijbg56qA0d0kPszXBhp">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.reddit.com/r/Deleuze/comments/1in80s0/what_do_you_make_of_the_famous_accelerate_the/?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805604174&amp;usg=AOvVaw0Tk22S_KagaMV1GWu0n36n">Reddit</ref></span><span class="c3">. Whether evangelicalism mutates again or collapses under its own contradictions will shape the spiritual terrain in which new (neo&#8209;pagan?) imaginaries must operate.</span></p><p class="c2"></p>

=== <span class="c5">Evangelicalism and the Neoliberal Order</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Contemporary U.S. evangelicalism operates largely as a </span><span class="c8">simplified faith culture</span><span>&nbsp;shaped for mass consumption. Services resemble entertainment events &ndash; with stadium&#8208;style praise bands, multimedia lighting, and rapid-fire sermons &ndash; rather than centers of rigorous theology. Even sympathetic observers admit the shallowness of much evangelical content. As pastor Tim Challies criticizes, many churches &ldquo;use clich&eacute;d words to worship a clich&eacute;d God&rdquo; so that congregants experience nothing deeper than sentimentality</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.challies.com/articles/the-shallowness-of-evangelicalism/%23:~:text%3DI%25E2%2580%2599m%2520sure%2520I%2520could%2520go,minds%2520and%2520to%2520our%2520hearts&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805605500&amp;usg=AOvVaw2_8A27g0FUblltMhzo7KtO">challies.com</ref></span><span>. This aestheticized worship discourages critical thought: emotional resonance and personal &ldquo;encounters with God&rdquo; replace extended biblical exposition or dialectical teaching. In effect, worship becomes a vehicle for ideological conformity. By offering distraction and an upbeat narrative of personal success, the format deters believers from questioning the social order. In Marxist terms, religion is a narcotic for the masses &ndash; &ldquo;the opium of the people&rdquo; &ndash; consoling them under capitalist exploitation</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://law.marquette.edu/facultyblog/2015/01/karl-marx-on-religion/comment-page-1/%23:~:text%3DMarx%25E2%2580%2599s%2520actual%2520words%2520regarding%2520religion,%25E2%2580%259D&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805606248&amp;usg=AOvVaw10TYs3qKefbXdDd0-rzB9T">law.marquette.edu</ref></span><span class="c3">. Contemporary evangelicalism exemplifies this, favoring simple uplifting messages over intellectual depth, thus channeling anxieties away from systemic critique into private piety.</span></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Patriarchy and the Neoliberal Family</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Evangelicalism continues to enforce strict </span><span class="c8">gender hierarchies</span><span>, buttressing the myth of the self-sufficient nuclear family even as its material basis erodes. Modern churches almost universally preach &ldquo;biblical manhood&rdquo; and female submission, reviving the patriarchal family of the 1950s. But with men&rsquo;s wages stagnant and dual-income households now the norm, this model is largely symbolic. Popular critics note that &ldquo;complementarianism is patriarchy&#8239;&ndash; nothing more, nothing less,&rdquo; despite evangelical claims to mutual &ldquo;complementarity&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://rachelheldevans.com/blog/complementarians-patriarchy%23:~:text%3DComplemenarianism%2520is%2520patriarchy%25E2%2580%2594nothing%2520more%252C%2520nothing,crystal%2520clear%2520when%2520John%2520Piper&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805607350&amp;usg=AOvVaw3mvgWhDPSnnbF8bsS8AL5c">rachelheldevans.com</ref></span><span>. In practice, women are often pressured into traditional roles and men into authoritarian &ldquo;head of household&rdquo; roles, even though economic reality forces both to work. This ideological insistence on male dominion (as &lsquo;God&rsquo;s design&rsquo;) and female deference stabilizes the </span><span class="c8">neoliberal family</span><span>&nbsp;ideal: the burden of care and responsibility falls on the private family so that the state may retreat. Maintaining these gender norms gives individuals a sense of order and purpose amid economic precarity. In sum, the </span><span class="c8">family values</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;promoted by evangelicals function as an ideological safeguard: they re-inscribe patriarchal authority on the cultural level precisely when genuine patriarchy (the breadwinning father) has been hollowed out by capitalism.</span></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Emotion and the Decline of Doctrine: Evangelism as Late-Stage Domination</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>In late-stage capitalism, evangelicalism has shifted from intellectual substance to affective spectacle &ndash; a transformation one can view through Deleuze&rsquo;s notion of &ldquo;pure control.&rdquo; The old </span><span class="c8">coded</span><span>&nbsp;doctrines (e.g. Calvinist theology) are </span><span class="c8">decoded</span><span>&nbsp;away, leaving a raw flow of feeling and belief that can be modulate by church producers. Churches now operate like entrepreneurial enterprises: pastors market the faith, worship is carefully stage-managed, and success is measured by crowd size and social-media buzz. David Wells, a theologian, notes how market logic has invaded worship: &ldquo;We have brought into the church the rhythms of buying and selling, of making a product appealing so that a potential buyer can be lured into a sale,&rdquo; and we turn &ldquo;the atmosphere of worship into one of pleasant entertainment&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/soul-shaping-reality-gospel-interview-david-wells%23:~:text%3DDW%253A%2520We%2520have%2520brought%2520into,takes%252C%2520no%2520matter%2520how%2520inappropriate&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805609386&amp;usg=AOvVaw2u5omS2uS5uAzNedCNVx78">learn.ligonier.org</ref></span><span>. The gospel becomes a spiritual product packaged as feel-good therapy. For Deleuze, this is a hallmark of capitalist &ldquo;societies of control&rdquo; &ndash; people are not controlled by overt discipline but by modulating their desires and affects. Evangelical services, with their upbeat music and positive-affirmation slogans, exemplify this mode. Content-light preaching (e.g. prosperity promises or simplistic moral lists) substitutes for dense theology. Believers are thus subtly governed by emotion: they are </span><span class="c6">led to love their situation</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;in exchange for community and hope, rather than confronted with material injustice. This embodies a late-stage ideological domination, where control is exercised not by heavy-handed doctrine but by constant stimulation and distraction.</span></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Homophobia, Transphobia, and the Politics of Identity</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Sexual and gender issues serve as </span><span class="c8">cultural battlefields</span><span>&nbsp;that &ldquo;make the base&rdquo; for evangelical political identity. With capitalist crisis undermining stable class identities, evangelicals increasingly fixate on policing sexuality as a source of order. Historian Randall Balmer explains that the Religious Right learned any issue tied to sexual morality would reliably mobilize its members: &ldquo;any issue that had some sort of connection to sexuality or sexual behavior was going to work for them&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/why-is-the-gop-escalating-attacks-on-trans-rights-experts-say-the-goal-is-to-make-sure-evangelicals-vote%23:~:text%3D%25E2%2580%259CAs%2520they%2520were%2520searching%2520for,them%252C%25E2%2580%259D%2520Balmer%2520told%2520The%252019th&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805611064&amp;usg=AOvVaw0wx26W1MgVOMODcfyS-LVz">pbs.org</ref></span><span>. Evangelical leaders cycle through crusades against &ldquo;sodomy,&rdquo; gay marriage, abortion, and now transgender rights, not simply out of doctrinal purity but to produce a cohesive &ldquo;us vs. them&rdquo; narrative. This culture war dynamic resonates with Marxist and Foucauldian ideas of scapegoating: as economic and social institutions destabilize, marginalized groups become convenient targets. One social theorist notes that in capitalist crises homophobia and transphobia are &ldquo;weaponized to police populations around access to diminishing spoils or social surpluses&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://jacobin.com/2023/06/capitalism-homophobia-history-christopher-chitty-sexual-hegemony%23:~:text%3DIn%2520those%2520contexts%252C%2520sodomy%2520accusations,uses%2520some%2520broad%2520histories%2520and&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805611853&amp;usg=AOvVaw0-KHuaRmBrm1XnSVeVXojg">jacobin.com</ref></span><span class="c3">. In practice, enraging the faithful over &ldquo;gender chaos&rdquo; helps maintain an illusion of cosmic order: rigid male/female roles are presented as God&rsquo;s unshakeable design against a world of fluid identities. In the wake of Roe v. Wade&rsquo;s repeal, this trend accelerated: evangelicals, having won on abortion, have redoubled their campaign on LGBT issues to channel discontent. The preached threat of &ldquo;men in women&rsquo;s bathrooms&rdquo; or &ldquo;groomers&rdquo; functions to discipline congregants&rsquo; anxieties and reinforce the old gender code, even as the real material basis for that code continues to vanish.</span></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">From Reformation to Megachurch: A Distorted Inheritance</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Modern evangelicalism would be unrecognizable to Luther or Calvin. The Reformers built denominations around doctrine, biblical exegesis, and a communal intellectual tradition. By contrast, today&rsquo;s megachurches emphasize </span><span class="c8">inward experience over theological rigor</span><span>, though they still demand inner belief. The only lasting legacy of Protestantism is the premium on personal faith (&ldquo;believe and be saved&rdquo;), yet this has been transmuted into a consumerized spirituality. David Wells argues that instead of confronting sin and society, the American church has largely become a &ldquo;marketing strategy&rdquo; for self-help</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/soul-shaping-reality-gospel-interview-david-wells%23:~:text%3Dbad%2521%2520What%2520it%2520requires%2520is,before%2520our%2520great%2520God%2520and&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805613505&amp;usg=AOvVaw1cJP14YGwJWjjroYQjYlLo">learn.ligonier.org</ref></span><span>. He insists that the true gospel &ldquo;is not about self-therapy&rdquo; but &ldquo;a soul-shaking, costly, demanding reality&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/soul-shaping-reality-gospel-interview-david-wells%23:~:text%3Dbad%2521%2520What%2520it%2520requires%2520is,before%2520our%2520great%2520God%2520and&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805613822&amp;usg=AOvVaw2FN6hQOwx3PxCZk5udHl18">learn.ligonier.org</ref></span><span>&nbsp;&ndash; a witness scarcely found in much of today&rsquo;s ministry. Where Lutherans and Calvinists would debate the Eucharist or predestination, many evangelicals now simply feel goosebumps when the lights dim, then move on to the next upbeat song. In short, the complex Protestant intellectual heritage has been </span><span class="c8">decoded</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;into something like a feel-good club, re-territorialized on hope and belonging. Structurally, however, evangelicals still demand loyalty to faith (echoing &ldquo;faith alone&rdquo;); there remains an insistence on an inner conversion experience. But even that inwardness is thin: it is inwardness as personal success story, not inwardness as humble submission to a transcendent truth.</span></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Transnational Networks and Anti-Communist Roots</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>The U.S. evangelical core is the hub of a </span><span class="c8">global religious&#8208;right</span><span>&nbsp;network united by shared ideology and anti-communist history. Even ostensibly non-evangelical groups like Japan&rsquo;s Unification Church have paralleled this agenda. In fact, Moon&rsquo;s Unification movement &ldquo;set up media companies, research centers, and educational institutions that focused on anti-communist ideologies&rdquo; in the 1950s&ndash;80s</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_Church_and_politics%23:~:text%3DIn%2520the%25201950s%2520and%252080s%252C,52%2520in%2520Japan%252C%2520leading%2520to&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805615306&amp;usg=AOvVaw12DH-yYPw9y3tVsgFkcUUR">en.wikipedia.org</ref></span><span class="c3">. Such groups forged ties with American conservatives (e.g. through the National Prayer Breakfast, founded by Abraham Vereide in 1953 as a Christian anti-Communist fellowship). Likewise, hardline Catholic organizations (Opus Dei and others) work alongside evangelicals in crusades against socialism, abortion, and secularism. These transnational alliances trace back to the Cold War: the Religious Right grew out of a &ldquo;spiritual-industrial complex&rdquo; aimed at defeating Marxism, using the rhetoric of a holy war to unite business leaders, pastors, and politicians. In practice, this means international conferences and family-value coalitions that blur denominational lines. The National Prayer Breakfast &ndash; an annual meeting of politicians, preachers, and foreign dignitaries &ndash; exemplifies this network in action. Across borders, evangelicals, Moonies, conservative Catholics, and right-wing Christians share resources and messaging, reinforcing each other&rsquo;s power. In each context, appeals to anti-communism and fear of &ldquo;moral decay&rdquo; form the backbone of an ideology that ultimately justifies the capitalist status quo.</span></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Global Parallels: Emerging Patterns in Other Traditions</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span class="c3">While our focus is U.S. evangelicalism, similar religion-capital alliances are seen elsewhere. For example, Turkey under Erdo&#287;an has promoted a state-centric Sunni Islam that validates neoliberal economics and patriarchal social policies. The government encourages &ldquo;faith-based&rdquo; charity and conservative education that push a family-centered vision mirroring America&rsquo;s &ldquo;family values,&rdquo; even as it embraces global capitalism. Scholars observe that many Islamic organizations in Turkey now function as instruments of neoliberal governmentality, disciplining women into traditional roles while integrating markets into daily life. In short, an &ldquo;Islamic neoliberalism&rdquo; is emerging: it shares with evangelicalism an emphasis on personal piety over social justice, and on reproducing existing hierarchies via moral authority. This is distinct from older &ldquo;overcoded&rdquo; forms like Wahhabi fundamentalism or state secularism; rather, it adapts religion to the demands of market society. Similar convergences can be seen in Hindu nationalism and other faith movements worldwide, where religion is recast to legitimate existing power structures while providing spiritual consolation.</span></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">Ideology and Affect: Theoretical Perspectives</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Drawing it all together, we can interpret evangelical capitalism with classic critical theories. </span><span class="c8">Althusser&rsquo;s interpellation</span><span>&nbsp;is strikingly on point: Christian ideology &ldquo;addresses a human individual called Peter&hellip; in order to tell you that God exists and that you are answerable to Him,&rdquo; ultimately declaring &ldquo;This is your place in the world! This is what you must do!&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://medium.com/religion-bites/louis-althusser-on-ideology-state-apparatus-ideology-interpellation-5a8b3df554d0%23:~:text%3DIt%2520says%253A%2520I%2520address%2520myself,means%252C%2520if%2520you%2520observe%2520the&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805618610&amp;usg=AOvVaw00hLfjADR3DZ0HQUnnfU1-">medium.com</ref></span><span>. In practice, sermons name congregants (even by name) and designate their roles (husband, wife, citizen), and believers respond, &ldquo;Yes, this is me.&rdquo; This ritual hailing ensures each person recognizes the evangelical life-script as their destiny. Althusser notes that such interpellation presupposes a single &ldquo;Absolute Other&rdquo; (God) whose authority grounds the whole system</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://medium.com/religion-bites/louis-althusser-on-ideology-state-apparatus-ideology-interpellation-5a8b3df554d0%23:~:text%3DIt%2520then%2520emerges%2520that%2520the,what%2520is%2520rightly%2520called%2520the&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805619240&amp;usg=AOvVaw30e4lInosepemBJP1_N9f8">medium.com</ref></span><span class="c3">.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>In Foucault&rsquo;s terms, the evangelical church is a </span><span class="c8">pastoral power</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;that produces self-disciplined subjects. From childhood Sunday school through voluntary adult Bible classes, believers learn to monitor their own conduct (sexual, financial, personal) by internalizing evangelical norms. Confession and accountability groups further instill this self-governance. In effect, the church trains &ldquo;docile bodies&rdquo; aligned to capitalist society: believers police themselves to be productive, faithful citizens and parents. There is no need for external force; spirituality itself instils the desired behavior.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>Walter Benjamin&rsquo;s insights on </span><span class="c8">aestheticized politics</span><span>&nbsp;also resonate. Benjamin argued that fascism turns politics into mass spectacle (&ldquo;the logical outcome of fascism is an aestheticization of political life&rdquo;)</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.commonwealmagazine.org/benjamins-warning%23:~:text%3D%25E2%2580%259CThe%2520logical%2520outcome%2520of%2520fascism,without%2520effect%252C%2520you%2520get%2520aesthetics&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805620621&amp;usg=AOvVaw3rz5BMXdsDlVWvIX3cyQhV">commonwealmagazine.org</ref></span><span>. Similarly, evangelicalism often merges religion and politics into an emotional pageant. Mega-rallies, patriotically charged sermons, and prayer rallies treat political-economic orders as moral crusades. By politicizing religion in aesthetic form (flags at church, rhetoric of &ldquo;righteous nation,&rdquo; culture-war marches), the movement channels dissent into spectacle rather than organized challenge. The effect is the same Benjamin described: people demand expression (e.g. a prayer rally) </span><span class="c6">without effect</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;on real power structures. Thus the evangelical Right&rsquo;s media-savvy events serve the status quo by satisfying the longing for change with gut-level theatrics.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>Finally, Lewis Mumford&rsquo;s </span><span class="c8">megamachine</span><span>&nbsp;concept highlights the technological-totalitarian dimension. Mumford called modern tech-capitalism &ldquo;the ultimate religion of our seemingly rational age,&rdquo; in which &ldquo;the meaning of life was reduced to accelerating movement and change&rdquo; and &ldquo;bigger and bigger&hellip; faster and faster became ends in themselves&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://librarianshipwreck.wordpress.com/2024/06/14/the-ultimate-religion-of-our-seemingly-rational-age-revisiting-mumfords-megamachine/%23:~:text%3DIn%2520commenting%2520on%2520%25E2%2580%259Cthe%2520myth,godlike%2520power%25E2%2580%259D%2520and%2520all%2520of&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805622047&amp;usg=AOvVaw0qwUt1kLO-rPR1aX57ghZr">librarianshipwreck.wordpress.com</ref></span><span class="c3">. Evangelicalism today inhabits that megatechnical environment. Digital streaming, social media algorithms, and consumer culture form a grand infrastructure that enfolds every church. Technology is worshipped alongside God (smartphones, megachurch sound systems, online influence). Evangelical media networks (TV preachers, podcasts, conference tours) are nodes of this megamachine. Believers are offered a steady stream of images and narratives of faith as remedy &ndash; a &ldquo;mass-produced plentitude&rdquo; as Mumford describes &ndash; which distracts from capitalism&rsquo;s harms. In short, the church is not separate from the megatechnical system but part of its priesthood. Evangelicalism&rsquo;s emphasis on individual salvation and trust in a &ldquo;higher plan&rdquo; functions in the same way Mumford saw blind faith in science and progress: it sustains the myth that the system can be redeemed (by God or technology) even as it grinds people under.</span></p><ul class="c14 lst-kix_973607v9i7pw-0 start"><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Marxism (ideology/opium)</span><span>: Religion is ideology that maintains class power. Evangelicalism preaches rewards in heaven to pacify earthly suffering</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://law.marquette.edu/facultyblog/2015/01/karl-marx-on-religion/comment-page-1/%23:~:text%3DMarx%25E2%2580%2599s%2520actual%2520words%2520regarding%2520religion,%25E2%2580%259D&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805623445&amp;usg=AOvVaw1lSFqHbduFeAoJqLBNQ1VP">law.marquette.edu</ref></span><span class="c3">. As Marx predicted, it soothes &ldquo;sighs of the oppressed&rdquo; instead of organizing them against exploitation.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Althusser (interpellation)</span><span>: Believers are hailed as subjects (&ldquo;Peter, this is your place!&rdquo;)</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://medium.com/religion-bites/louis-althusser-on-ideology-state-apparatus-ideology-interpellation-5a8b3df554d0%23:~:text%3DIt%2520says%253A%2520I%2520address%2520myself,means%252C%2520if%2520you%2520observe%2520the&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805624022&amp;usg=AOvVaw212EvY1pnF2RRAKkO2DAHj">medium.com</ref></span><span class="c3">&nbsp;and accept fixed identities. Evangelical authority is essentially god&rsquo;s &ldquo;voiceless&rdquo; hail rendered in pulpit form.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Foucault (discipline)</span><span class="c3">: The church disciplines the soul. Via confession, guilt, and ecclesial surveillance, Christians internalize moral norms and police themselves to fit capitalist society.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Benjamin (aestheticization)</span><span>: Evangelical politics is ritual spectacle. Worship and crusades aestheticize values (freedom, family, patriotism) to preserve the status quo</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.commonwealmagazine.org/benjamins-warning%23:~:text%3D%25E2%2580%259CThe%2520logical%2520outcome%2520of%2520fascism,without%2520effect%252C%2520you%2520get%2520aesthetics&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805624840&amp;usg=AOvVaw0RQ2DNrDx6GV3LCCwhdvYH">commonwealmagazine.org</ref></span><span class="c3">. Emotions substitute for democratic deliberation.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Mumford (megamachine)</span><span>: Technology is the hidden church. Modern tech becomes a secular deity whose &ldquo;accelerating change&rdquo; is worshipped in place of social change</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://librarianshipwreck.wordpress.com/2024/06/14/the-ultimate-religion-of-our-seemingly-rational-age-revisiting-mumfords-megamachine/%23:~:text%3DIn%2520commenting%2520on%2520%25E2%2580%259Cthe%2520myth,godlike%2520power%25E2%2580%259D%2520and%2520all%2520of&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805625396&amp;usg=AOvVaw12IpCYZmPAG2ES9067w1HJ">librarianshipwreck.wordpress.com</ref></span><span class="c3">. Evangelical media and consumer rituals are the contemporary megatechnical cult keeping the system in place.<br></span></li></ul><p class="c0"><span>In summary, evangelicalism today functions as an </span><span class="c8">ideological apparatus</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;that keeps capitalist relations running smoothly by saturating life with spectacles of faith and rigid moral codes. It interpellates believers into predefined roles (patriarch/provider, submissive wife, obedient child, God-fearing worker) and disciplines them with promise of afterlife as the ultimate payout. Its religious aesthetics mirror those of consumer capitalism: flashy, immediate, emotionally satisfying, yet substantively empty. Through these means, U.S. evangelicalism promotes the capitalist status quo and legitimizes exploitation under a veneer of piety &ndash; an alliance of religion, desire, and power that only intensifies as late-stage capitalism advances.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Sources:</span><span>&nbsp;Analysis above draws on contemporary and classical sources of political theology and critical theory, including evangelical commentators</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.challies.com/articles/the-shallowness-of-evangelicalism/%23:~:text%3DI%25E2%2580%2599m%2520sure%2520I%2520could%2520go,minds%2520and%2520to%2520our%2520hearts&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805626732&amp;usg=AOvVaw0XIYZlG1DMUex8H0D80OMr">challies.com</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/soul-shaping-reality-gospel-interview-david-wells%23:~:text%3DDW%253A%2520We%2520have%2520brought%2520into,takes%252C%2520no%2520matter%2520how%2520inappropriate&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805626909&amp;usg=AOvVaw2LTFFlwpoPgi-sEoNm17h7">learn.ligonier.org</ref></span><span>&nbsp;and left critiques</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://jacobin.com/2023/06/capitalism-homophobia-history-christopher-chitty-sexual-hegemony%23:~:text%3DIn%2520those%2520contexts%252C%2520sodomy%2520accusations,uses%2520some%2520broad%2520histories%2520and&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805627138&amp;usg=AOvVaw058hGm_dU-lRxqv4AnK3fX">jacobin.com</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://librarianshipwreck.wordpress.com/2024/06/14/the-ultimate-religion-of-our-seemingly-rational-age-revisiting-mumfords-megamachine/%23:~:text%3DIn%2520commenting%2520on%2520%25E2%2580%259Cthe%2520myth,godlike%2520power%25E2%2580%259D%2520and%2520all%2520of&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805627351&amp;usg=AOvVaw1Bw6liJyUxR6K7ZtMG0C3E">librarianshipwreck.wordpress.com</ref></span><span>, integrated with theoretical insights from Althusser, Foucault, Benjamin, and Mumford</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://librarianshipwreck.wordpress.com/2024/06/14/the-ultimate-religion-of-our-seemingly-rational-age-revisiting-mumfords-megamachine/%23:~:text%3DIn%2520commenting%2520on%2520%25E2%2580%259Cthe%2520myth,godlike%2520power%25E2%2580%259D%2520and%2520all%2520of&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805627982&amp;usg=AOvVaw3JPoIi18qPENKbtndGI5JH">librarianshipwreck.wordpress.com</ref></span><span === <span class="c5">Chapter 8</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span class="c22 c8 c23">Re&#8209;Enchanting the Marketplace: Early Mormonism as Communal, Cosmic, and Counter&#8209;Capitalist</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c6">&ldquo;As man now&#8239;is, God once&#8239;was; as God now&#8239;is, man may&#8239;be.&rdquo;</span><span>&nbsp;&mdash;Lorenzo Snow (1840s)</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.mormonwiki.com/As_Man_Now_Is%252C_God_Once_Was?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805628763&amp;usg=AOvVaw2AyGpyyRIiwd7aGl7Pzqz1">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.mormonwiki.com/As_Man_Now_Is%252C_God_Once_Was?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805628924&amp;usg=AOvVaw2E4DUQJ-ekOExjV2DdTqom">mormonwiki.com</ref></span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">1 Introduction: The Strange Career of the Latter&#8209;day Saints</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Nineteenth&#8209;century Mormonism erupted out of the Protestant &ldquo;burned&#8209;over district&rdquo; yet immediately </span><span class="c8">rejected the disenchanted cosmos</span><span>&nbsp;that mainline revivalism had normalized. &nbsp;Joseph Smith&rsquo;s revelations insisted that </span><span class="c6">all</span><span>&nbsp;matter is eternal, that gods progress, and that humanity may join their ranks. This audacious cosmology fuelled experiments in consecrated property, plural marriage, and theocratic settlement&mdash;practices that, at their inception, looked more like </span><span class="c8">utopian socialism</span><span>&nbsp;than the bourgeois respectability later associated with Utah. Whereas Marx denounced religion as ideology, early Latter&#8209;day Saints weaponised myth to build a counter&#8209;economy; they tried to </span><span class="c8">reterritorialise</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;the capitalist frontier on communal lines even as they borrowed its techniques of movement and expansion.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c3">We read Mormonism here through four lenses:</span></p><ul class="c14 lst-kix_25a4ywbr123e-0 start"><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Marx &amp; primitive accumulation</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;&ndash; Mormon consecration fought enclosure with a covenantal commons.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Deleuze &amp; Guattari&rsquo;s &ldquo;re&#8209;enchantment machine&rdquo;</span><span>&nbsp;&ndash; Smith decoded Protestantism only to replug believers into an </span><span class="c6">infinitely expandable</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;cosmos.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Walter Benjamin&rsquo;s dialectical image</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;&ndash; the Nauvoo temple as a revolutionary montage of Israelite, Masonic, and American symbols.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c8">Lewis Mumford&rsquo;s &ldquo;megamachine&rdquo;</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;&ndash; Brigham Young&rsquo;s territorial kingdom anticipates the technocratic state yet briefly subordinates it to agrarian cooperation.<br></span></li></ul><hr><p class="c2"></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">2 Cosmos Reclaimed: Eternal Matter and the Adam&#8209;God Turn</span> ===

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">2.1 Material Spirit and Eternal Progress</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Smith&rsquo;s May 1843 discourse declared that </span><span class="c6">&ldquo;spirit is a refined matter&rdquo;</span><span>&nbsp;and that intelligence &ldquo;cannot be created or made&rdquo;</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.josephsmithpapers.org/paper-summary/discourse-17-may-1843-b?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805631838&amp;usg=AOvVaw3phmtxYM_HMLfHFjw43jIS">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.josephsmithpapers.org/paper-summary/discourse-17-may-1843-b?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805632075&amp;usg=AOvVaw1v8Kg8h3IE3FEWURlNnmzh">josephsmithpapers.org</ref></span><span>. Matter itself is divine; the world is </span><span class="c8">enchanted down to its atoms</span><span>. Snow&rsquo;s famous couplet turns this into eschatology: humans may ascend the same ontological ladder God once climbed. Where classical Christianity saw an unbridgeable Creator&#8209;creature gap, Mormonism installs a </span><span class="c8">cosmic proletariat</span><span class="c3">: every being can rise by cooperative labor&mdash;temple work, covenant, and family sealing.</span></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">2.2 The Adam&#8209;God Doctrine as Radical Genealogy</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Brigham Young&rsquo;s sermons went further: </span><span class="c6">&ldquo;Adam is our Father and God&hellip; the God of the earth&rdquo;</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.mormonthink.com/QUOTES/adamgod.htm?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805632974&amp;usg=AOvVaw095ZGCRYqJC85-yY1_YeB1">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.mormonthink.com/QUOTES/adamgod.htm?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805633112&amp;usg=AOvVaw2tgYDo6j3bKvJ68b9nRCh6">mormonthink.com</ref></span><span>. Scholars debate the doctrine&rsquo;s orthodoxy, but politically it </span><span class="c8">relocated sovereignty</span><span>&nbsp;from a distant omnipotence to the first embodied patriarch. In Deleuzian terms, Young folds divinity back into the plane of immanence, short&#8209;circuiting the transcendent despotic signifier. God becomes an </span><span class="c8">ancestor&#8209;king</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;whose authority is genealogical rather than absolutist&mdash;a move that both empowers communal kin&#8209;structures and risks reinforcing patriarchal domination.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">3 Consecration, the United Orders, and Anti&#8209;Capitalist Praxis</span> ===

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">3.1 Law of Consecration</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Revelations of 1831 introduced a covenant to </span><span class="c8">&ldquo;hold all things in common&rdquo;</span><span>&nbsp;and appoint bishops as stewards</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/history/topics/consecration-and-stewardship?lang%3Deng%26utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805634324&amp;usg=AOvVaw02YqNZ7cPyVpx64THdavb_">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/history/topics/consecration-and-stewardship?lang%3Deng%26utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805634510&amp;usg=AOvVaw2E3PBGTiQSN9VYja7bTn3v">churchofjesuschrist.org</ref></span><span>. Private property was to be subordinated to need; surplus redistributed. This resembles the </span><span class="c6">primitive Christian communism</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;of Acts and echoes Fourierist and Owenite experiments sprouting across America.</span></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">3.2 United Orders as Communal Corporations</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>From Kirtland (1830s) to Brigham City (1870s) the church organised </span><span class="c8">United Orders</span><span>&mdash;civic&#8209;economic co&#8209;ops where families deeded land to a common fund and received stewardships in return</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/history/topics/united-orders?lang%3Deng%26utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805635318&amp;usg=AOvVaw3B-IjsmhiX9-wREPM5mOB1">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/history/topics/united-orders?lang%3Deng%26utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805635494&amp;usg=AOvVaw1ohHl7D6Yl_yEPafUdIHzs">churchofjesuschrist.org</ref></span><span class="c3">. These orders:</span></p><ul class="c14 lst-kix_u5unn74ef5b9-0 start"><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c3">Abolished wage labour among saints.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c3">Fixed prices collectively to undercut speculators.<br></span></li><li class="c0 c12 li-bullet-0"><span class="c3">Instituted bishop&rsquo;s storehouses as proto&#8209;welfare.<br></span></li></ul><p class="c0"><span>Marx might read this as an </span><span class="c8">anti&#8209;enclosure revolt</span><span class="c3">: a frontier commons against national banks and railroad capital. Yet the Orders collapsed under federal pressure, internal inequality, and Utah&rsquo;s integration into transcontinental markets&mdash;illustrating Benjamin&rsquo;s insight that every revolutionary &ldquo;image&rdquo; is shot through with its counter&#8209;image of defeat.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">4 Contradictions: Polygyny, Patriarchy, and the Color Line</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Radical cosmology coexisted with </span><span class="c8">radical patriarchy</span><span>. Plural marriage concentrated authority in male priesthood; the Adam&#8209;God myth literalised male divinity. Simultaneously, Brigham Young codified a </span><span class="c8">priesthood/racial ban</span><span>&nbsp;(1852&ndash;1978) that excluded Black saints from temple rites</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_people_and_temple_and_priesthood_policies_in_the_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805637108&amp;usg=AOvVaw19SJKDbA_mTxOoLgQtWXQZ">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_people_and_temple_and_priesthood_policies_in_the_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805637302&amp;usg=AOvVaw3GSZjSc1kqIZi9oEkE2km5">Wikipedia</ref></span><span class="c3">. Thus a movement born in communitarian aspiration reproduced settler hierarchies&mdash;an ambivalence Deleuze would call the &ldquo;simultaneity of deterritorialisation and reterritorialisation.&rdquo;</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">5 Comparative Interlude</span> ===

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">5.1 State Shinto and Imperial Theosis</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Meiji leaders nationalised Shinto in 1868, enthroning the Emperor as living deity to mobilise agrarian subjects for industrial empire</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.britannica.com/topic/State-Shinto?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805638125&amp;usg=AOvVaw25Wt9UNJKbVTjqK7jg9MXN">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.britannica.com/topic/State-Shinto?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805638279&amp;usg=AOvVaw372LLSC8dnJa5OhfJi8ydB">Encyclopedia Britannica</ref></span><span>. Like Mormonism, State&#8239;Shinto used genealogy (sun&#8209;descended Tenn&#333;) and temple ritual to sacralise settlement (Hokkaid&#333;) and communal labour. Both projects fused </span><span class="c8">myth with colonisation</span><span class="c3">, but where State Shinto enforced hierarchy, early Mormonism preached lay theosis and voluntary consecration.</span></p>

==== <span class="c13 c7 c8">5.2 God&#8209;Building under Soviet Socialism</span> ====
<p class="c0"><span>Lunacharsky&rsquo;s </span><span class="c8">bogostroitel&rsquo;stvo</span><span>&nbsp;sought an atheist civic cult harnessing ritual and myth for proletarian uplift</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God-Building?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805639075&amp;usg=AOvVaw1BGfOADU8_BzoRBy9xAPjp">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God-Building?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805639208&amp;usg=AOvVaw2F-HUizGUcOWa0A7-rbwPW">Wikipedia</ref></span><span>. Mormon temple liturgy&mdash;with its Masonic dramas and covenantal oaths&mdash;already performed a similar </span><span class="c8">myth&#8209;engineering</span><span>, but in a theistic register. Both movements reveal how modern projects &mdash;imperial, socialist, or sectarian&mdash;turn to </span><span class="c8">new theurgies</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;when Enlightenment rationality proves cold.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

=== <span class="c13 c19 c8">6 From Kingdom of God to Corporation of the President</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Railroads, federal anti&#8209;polygamy campaigns, and the 1890 Manifesto forced Utah&rsquo;s integration. By the mid&#8209;20th century the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter&#8209;day Saints had become one of America&rsquo;s wealthiest corporations, investing in media, insurance, and global real estate. The communal Orders were replaced by </span><span class="c8">tithing and for&#8209;profit subsidiaries</span><span>; polygamy was renounced; racial bans persisted until 1978. Mumford&rsquo;s &ldquo;megamachine&rdquo; triumphs: the church now operates data centers and maintains an online genealogy empire&mdash;redeeming the dead with </span><span class="c8">cloud computing</span><span>&nbsp;rather than agrarian commons. Cosmic optimism survives, but the cooperative economy has been thoroughly </span><span class="c8">reterritorialised by finance capital</span><span class="c3">.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

=== <span class="c13 c8 c19">7 Conclusion: A Dialectical Legacy</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Early Mormonism dramatises a recurring theme in this book: attempts to </span><span class="c8">re&#8209;enchant</span><span>&nbsp;and </span><span class="c8">re&#8209;common</span><span>&nbsp;the world under capitalist pressure. Smith&rsquo;s material cosmology and the United Orders were genuine gestures toward what Benjamin called </span><span class="c6">&ldquo;the weak messianic power&rdquo;</span><span>&nbsp;of the oppressed. Yet patriarchal and racial exclusions, plus the irresistible pull of westward markets, foreclosed the most radical possibilities. Today, LDS humanitarianism and missionary networks mirror neoliberal NGO logic, while temple theology still whispers the old promise of godhood. Mormonism thus stands as a </span><span class="c8">dialectical image</span><span class="c3">&mdash;at once a frontier socialism and a template for corporate religion&mdash;offering both caution and inspiration to contemporary movements seeking to reclaim myth and economics from the dead hand of capital.</span></p><hr><p class="c2"></p>

</span><span class="c6">Wikipedia</span><span>&nbsp;(accessed 2025).</span><span><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_people_and_temple_and_priesthood_policies_in_the_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805645643&amp;usg=AOvVaw0eDVuISoa2vcTZR7lBGyUh">&nbsp;</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_people_and_temple_and_priesthood_policies_in_the_Church_of_Jesus_Christ_of_Latter-day_Saints?utm_source%3Dchatgpt.com&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805645805&amp;usg=AOvVaw146KxXgtj4ah5_kdt4wJt8">Wikipedia</ref></span></li></ul><p class="c2"></p>

=== <span class="c5">Cosmic Enchantment and Zion Ideal: Early Mormonism as Utopian Reform</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Early Mormonism emerged in the 1830s as a radically </span><span class="c6">re</span><span>-enchanted vision of Christianity. In Weberian terms, Joseph Smith embodied </span><span class="c8">charismatic authority</span><span>&nbsp;&ndash; a living prophet whose revelations transformed theology and social organization</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://bycommonconsent.com/2016/04/21/on-the-routinization-bureaucratization-and-correlation-of-charisma-max-weber-and-the-mormons/%23:~:text%3Dexplicitly%2520invokes%2520Joseph%2520Smith%2520and,%25E2%2580%259Ccharisma%252C%25E2%2580%259D%2520which%2520he%2520defines%2520as&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805646683&amp;usg=AOvVaw3j5HaUyjX253tplP0il778">bycommonconsent.com</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://bycommonconsent.com/2016/04/21/on-the-routinization-bureaucratization-and-correlation-of-charisma-max-weber-and-the-mormons/%23:~:text%3DBut%2520Weber%2520can%2520help%2520us,that%2520are%2520also%2520very%2520real&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805646902&amp;usg=AOvVaw3K0gAVGF_jXha7aP6UJ43V">bycommonconsent.com</ref></span><span>. Unlike Protestant individual salvation, Smith&rsquo;s revelations envisioned a </span><span class="c8">physical cosmos</span><span>&nbsp;imbued with sacred meaning. In Mormon doctrine all intelligence and matter are eternal &ndash; &ldquo;God is an Architect of the material universe, not the Source of all things&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.mrm.org/ex-nihilo%23:~:text%3DAccording%2520to%2520LDS%2520teaching%252C%2520finite,is%2520limited%2520by%2520natural%2520law&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805647354&amp;usg=AOvVaw2mjKxSzsKACsHh7eUfQ2L8">mrm.org</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.mrm.org/ex-nihilo%23:~:text%3DSecond%2520President%2520Brigham%2520Young%2520took,Journal%2520of%2520Discourses%252014%253A116&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805647505&amp;usg=AOvVaw1R5VfhCm2l9qyorhCHZqsE">mrm.org</ref></span><span>. Thus God and man share the same kind of substance: early Mormons taught that humans are literally &ldquo;gods in embryo,&rdquo; destined to progress eternally toward divine fullness</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.dialoguejournal.com/wp-content/uploads/sbi/articles/Dialogue_V50N03_14.pdf%23:~:text%3D46%2520Dialogue%252C%2520Fall%25202017%2520This,is%2520true%2520of%2520Mormon%2520monism&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805647864&amp;usg=AOvVaw0n7qFLatNlSuzku_AoIwwN">dialoguejournal.com</ref></span><span>. Brigham Young even preached the controversial &ldquo;Adam&ndash;God&rdquo; theory &ndash; that the first man Adam was himself God the Father</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.fairlatterdaysaints.org/answers/Brigham_Young_and_Adam-God_theory%23:~:text%3DBrigham%2520Young%2520taught%2520that%2520Adam%252C,man%252C%2520was%2520God%2520the%2520Father&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805648217&amp;usg=AOvVaw0zfQW-C_4QX69f1YzNBiki">fairlatterdaysaints.org</ref></span><span>&nbsp;&ndash; a startling affirmation of Mormon pantheon. These doctrines re-enchanted the world: nature and history were charged with mythic significance, and the temple was imagined as a direct pattern of heaven on earth (Eliade&rsquo;s </span><span class="c6">sacred space</span><span>). As Mircea Eliade observed, religious rites recreate a primordial &ldquo;mythic time&rdquo;; LDS temple ceremonies explicitly dramatize creation&ndash;fall&ndash;exaltation myths, sanctifying place and moment</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2004/08/eliade-mormonism-and-theories-of-religion-v/%23:~:text%3Dsome%2520of%2520his%2520major%2520insights,reference%2520point%2520for%2520the%2520city&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805648881&amp;usg=AOvVaw2LDvNm-39dwdPgtfewDyPu">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span class="c3">. In this early phase the universe was not a bare mechanism but a living cosmos of gods, spirits, and humans evolving together.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>Concretely, this re-enchantment included </span><span class="c8">planets, angels, and multiple worlds</span><span>. The Book of Abraham (LDS scripture) describes councils of gods organizing matter to build worlds</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.mrm.org/ex-nihilo%23:~:text%3DThe%2520LDS%2520scripture%2520Book%2520of,others%255D%2520may%2520dwell.%25E2%2580%259D&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805649437&amp;usg=AOvVaw2S68BfNjA98z0d7uBpIw9B">mrm.org</ref></span><span>. Joseph Smith taught that every righteous man receives a kingdom and may &ldquo;increase in glory&rdquo; forever. This cosmic theology contrasts sharply with the &ldquo;disenchanted&rdquo; world of 19th&#8209;century Protestant liberalism (Weber&rsquo;s secular age) &ndash; Mormonism insisted on </span><span class="c6">eternal progression</span><span>&nbsp;and a material universe, defying the notion that spirit is immaterial or distant</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.mrm.org/ex-nihilo%23:~:text%3DAccording%2520to%2520LDS%2520teaching%252C%2520finite,is%2520limited%2520by%2520natural%2520law&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805649964&amp;usg=AOvVaw1ONC-4OgIJE1oRbROUyyX7">mrm.org</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.dialoguejournal.com/wp-content/uploads/sbi/articles/Dialogue_V50N03_14.pdf%23:~:text%3D46%2520Dialogue%252C%2520Fall%25202017%2520This,is%2520true%2520of%2520Mormon%2520monism&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805650139&amp;usg=AOvVaw1Zxu_EBmA2X1lX236THh_R">dialoguejournal.com</ref></span><span class="c3">.</span></p>

=== <span class="c5">Communal Zion and Anti-Capitalist Praxis</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Early Mormons did not just dream; they acted on utopian ideals. The </span><span class="c8">Book of Mormon</span><span>&nbsp;itself envisions an &ldquo;ideal society&rdquo; where &ldquo;there were no poor among them&rdquo; because &ldquo;all things [were] common&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2009/02/mormonism-and-communal-studies/%23:~:text%3DNineteenth,family%2520by%2520embracing%2520plural%2520marriage&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805650797&amp;usg=AOvVaw3oyZL1MK-4ko5nV_2n6Msz">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span>. In practice Joseph Smith ordained a </span><span class="c8">Law of Consecration</span><span>: followers deeded property to the Church and received </span><span class="c6">stewardships</span><span>&nbsp;of land. In Kirtland (Ohio) and Missouri (1830s), Latter-day Saints attempted quasi-communist communities based on these revelations</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2009/02/mormonism-and-communal-studies/%23:~:text%3DWhile%2520communalism%2520deeply%2520influenced%2520Mormonism,day%2520Saints%252C%2520including%2520Brigham%2520Young&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805651325&amp;usg=AOvVaw1YUAYGhI24xADBjoiz-lTK">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span>. Inspired by millennial egalitarianism, they set up cooperative businesses, shared livestock and tools, and even started the Kirtland Safety Society bank as a communal credit venture. Later, under Brigham Young in Utah, dozens of </span><span class="c8">United Order</span><span>&nbsp;settlements were launched: local wards deeded property to the bishop and held &ldquo;stewardships,&rdquo; returning surplus production to a communal storehouse</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Order%23:~:text%3DThe%2520United%2520Order%2520established%2520egalitarian,which&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805651892&amp;usg=AOvVaw3zdSdHBRrizP5aBVhaBzVp">en.wikipedia.org</ref></span><span>. These egalitarian communities aimed to eliminate poverty and dependence on outsider markets &ndash; &ldquo;free the Mormons from dependence on outside merchants, and eliminate poverty&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2009/02/mormonism-and-communal-studies/%23:~:text%3DIn%2520Utah%252C%2520Mormons%2520engaged%2520in,In%2520the%2520late%25201800s&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805652287&amp;usg=AOvVaw3L3wnE-fSC_9A-1Q2tpkuD">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span class="c3">.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>This communalism explicitly opposed the new market capitalism of the age. As one historian notes, most 19th&#8209;century Mormonism &ldquo;rejected capitalist development and preached Christian communalism&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.religioussocialism.org/excavating_socialist_thought_in_mormonism_re_reading_hugh_nibley%23:~:text%3DStill%252C%2520times%2520can%2520change,%25E2%2580%259D&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805652745&amp;usg=AOvVaw17Qn5QfMNJiBc1ohQRZOgA">religioussocialism.org</ref></span><span>. Mormons had suffered through Jacksonian market crashes and land speculation; in response they built communal storehouses, welfare kitchens, and joint labor projects (including relief farming and company towns). Young even declared &ldquo;I will cut deeper than the ancients: they proposed to be equal, I propose to give equal&rdquo; (paraphrased from Brigham). The United Orders and </span><span class="c8">Zion projects</span><span>&nbsp;resembled other utopian socialist experiments (e.g. Owenite or Shaker communities), challenging &ldquo;fundamental ideals&rdquo; of American society &ndash; private property, republican politics, capitalist competition, and monogamous family norms</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2009/02/mormonism-and-communal-studies/%23:~:text%3Dthroughout%2520American%2520history%252C%2520these%2520groups,the%2520American%2520reaction%2520to%2520Mormonism&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805653728&amp;usg=AOvVaw2c4I-2G0aPcAl7J5PV0TTE">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2009/02/mormonism-and-communal-studies/%23:~:text%3DNineteenth,family%2520by%2520embracing%2520plural%2520marriage&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805653935&amp;usg=AOvVaw0ENcE1_IjNpXXaKQgYIDFl">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span>. Plural marriage itself broke bourgeois conventions of the family. In short, Mormonism offered a </span><span class="c6">nearly communistic</span><span>&nbsp;alternative: pooled resources, centralized planning by local bishops, and the credo of &ldquo;no poor among them&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2009/02/mormonism-and-communal-studies/%23:~:text%3DWhile%2520communalism%2520deeply%2520influenced%2520Mormonism,day%2520Saints%252C%2520including%2520Brigham%2520Young&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805654389&amp;usg=AOvVaw1jkKx7VyxGNb2tK2qkUJzz">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Order%23:~:text%3DThe%2520United%2520Order%2520established%2520egalitarian,which&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805654530&amp;usg=AOvVaw2ydmUwwfXQKfLzYkV7cNNp">en.wikipedia.org</ref></span><span class="c3">.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>Marxist anthropology would note that early Mormon Zion sought to create a classless &ldquo;Kingdom of God&rdquo; on earth, presaging aspects of socialism. Church intellectuals like Hugh Nibley later lamented that the modern church abandoned these values</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.religioussocialism.org/excavating_socialist_thought_in_mormonism_re_reading_hugh_nibley%23:~:text%3DHugh%2520Nibley%252C%2520a%2520long,but%2520aligning&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805655091&amp;usg=AOvVaw2tIetqZazpjkUzmnMxVe52">religioussocialism.org</ref></span><span>. By the 1890s, under outside pressure (polygamy prosecutions, federal taxes) most communal programs ceased and Utah joined the U.S.; Mormons &ldquo;embrac[ed] market capitalism&rdquo; to survive</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2009/02/mormonism-and-communal-studies/%23:~:text%3Dgoods%252C%2520and%2520the%2520disruption%2520of,by%2520the%2520church%2520welfare%2520program&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805655502&amp;usg=AOvVaw0bDLjCh3BsDLyrEi8mdqLV">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span>. The United Orders disappeared in mainstream LDS life (surviving only in fringe fundamentalist sects</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Order%23:~:text%3DThe%2520United%2520Order%2520is%2520not,70%2520United%2520Order%2520Family%2520of&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805655856&amp;usg=AOvVaw0qMVeBwVAI9F0UpGafPI5e">en.wikipedia.org</ref></span><span>), and Church leaders publicly denounced socialism. What remained of communalism was absorbed into the Church welfare and self-reliance system (a moderated version of Zion&rsquo;s charities)</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2009/02/mormonism-and-communal-studies/%23:~:text%3Dgoods%252C%2520and%2520the%2520disruption%2520of,by%2520the%2520church%2520welfare%2520program&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805656292&amp;usg=AOvVaw2NTjnLGkTwI_v1KJEar5Sd">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span class="c3">. In Marx&rsquo;s terms, the early Mormon &ldquo;base&rdquo; (property relations) shifted back into the capitalist superstructure, and religion now began to reinforce rather than challenge the existing order.</span></p>

=== <span class="c5">Theocratic Kingdom and Mythic History</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Parallel to economic communalism was an ambitious </span><span class="c8">theocratic vision</span><span>. Joseph Smith conceived a future &ldquo;Kingdom of God&rdquo; on earth, blending civil and sacred authority. In 1844 he organized the secret </span><span class="c8">Council of Fifty</span><span>, whose purpose was explicitly &ldquo;to symbolize and represent a future </span><span class="c6">theocratic</span><span>&nbsp;or </span><span class="c6">theodemocratic</span><span>&nbsp;Kingdom of God on the earth&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Fifty%23:~:text%3D,the%2520Second%2520Coming%2520of%2520Jesus&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805657337&amp;usg=AOvVaw3kVEiK5NZlNDg3luR3R31y">en.wikipedia.org</ref></span><span>. Smith even ran for U.S. President on a platform of restoring liberty under God. The Council&rsquo;s records speak of a coming millennial polity in which Christ would reign, and Smith foresaw Mormons governing a New Jerusalem. (LDS teaching held that during the Millennium Jesus will be &ldquo;king of this new world government,&rdquo; whose structure was planned to be quasi-republican</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Fifty%23:~:text%3DSmith%2520%2520in%25201844%2520to,the%2520%252054%2520of%2520Jesus&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805657896&amp;usg=AOvVaw1RhQJVW0a8VFcDhq6m0Cvo">en.wikipedia.org</ref></span><span class="c3">.) In 19th&#8209;century Mormon talk, America&rsquo;s Constitution was &ldquo;of no worth&rdquo; after the Millennium and the Saints would build Zion according to celestial law.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>This messianic-political impulse was fundamentally </span><span class="c8">mythic</span><span>&nbsp;in Eliade&rsquo;s sense: it framed time as a cycle of sacred eras. Early Latter&#8209;day Saints saw themselves living out the dramatis personae of scriptures (Book of Mormon, Bible, Revelation). The temple endowment ceremony, introduced in Nauvoo, reenacted the Edenic creation, the fall, and the gathering of Israel &ndash; literally bringing the preterrestrial &ldquo;plan of salvation&rdquo; into ritual time. Eliade would note that such rituals create an </span><span class="c8">eternal return</span><span>&nbsp;to primordial time; indeed LDS temples were designed as terrestrial reflections of heaven (the Salt Lake Temple as an </span><span class="c6">axis mundi</span><span>&nbsp;in the city)</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2004/08/eliade-mormonism-and-theories-of-religion-v/%23:~:text%3Dsome%2520of%2520his%2520major%2520insights,reference%2520point%2520for%2520the%2520city&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805659031&amp;usg=AOvVaw1eF06F4fe4Geg0JhbIye30">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span>. Adam&rsquo;s story, Elijah&rsquo;s powers, and the eventual return of Enoch and Zion were all taught as imminent realities. In short, early Mormonism was steeped in </span><span class="c8">mythic cosmology</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;&ndash; a sacred history that unfolded across ages (pre&#8209;existence, mortality, Millennium) rather than the linear demystified history of Enlightenment Protestantism.</span></p>

=== <span class="c5">Routinizing Revelation: From Charisma to Bureaucracy</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>Marxist and Weberian theory illuminate how this cosmic, radical movement then transformed into a modern institution. Weber described how &ldquo;charismatic&rdquo; movements must institutionalize or perish. Mormon history epitomizes this: after Smith&rsquo;s martyrdom the church faced the Weberian task of translating &ldquo;ground&#8209;breaking and world&#8209;making revelations into a set of handbooks and teacher&rsquo;s manuals&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://bycommonconsent.com/2016/04/21/on-the-routinization-bureaucratization-and-correlation-of-charisma-max-weber-and-the-mormons/%23:~:text%3DBut%2520Weber%2520can%2520help%2520us,that%2520are%2520also%2520very%2520real&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805660229&amp;usg=AOvVaw3QGhMBusTmHvGtiGVCH2BR">bycommonconsent.com</ref></span><span>. By the late 19th century Brigham Young and successors turned the church into a </span><span class="c8">bureaucratic organization</span><span class="c3">. Revelation was disciplined into coded scriptures (Doctrine &amp; Covenants) and rules; the living prophet&rsquo;s role was reserved to a First Presidency with a quorum of twelve apostles; local government and education came under church auspices. The charismatic frenzy of Missouri or Kirtland was tamed by new legitimacy claims: prophetic heritage, scriptural canon, and sacred ordinances.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>The 20th century saw further routinization. Under leaders like David O. McKay and especially during the &ldquo;Era of Standardization&rdquo; (circa 1960s&ndash;70s), the Church consolidated authority into a global bureaucracy. A </span><span class="c8">correlation program</span><span>&nbsp;systematized all lesson manuals, budgets, and publications under priesthood oversight</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://bycommonconsent.com/2017/07/06/death-by-correlation-committee/%23:~:text%3Dculminating%2520in%2520the%25201960s%252C%2520a,teachers%2520in%2520the%2520church%2520are&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805661622&amp;usg=AOvVaw1-oVPneEqeCusARN6TKWeR">bycommonconsent.com</ref></span><span>. As one insider laments, this &ldquo;huge effort&hellip;to amass all leadership, budgets, publications, and teaching materials under one hierarchical&hellip;umbrella&rdquo; sought uniformity at the cost of doctrinal breadth</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://bycommonconsent.com/2017/07/06/death-by-correlation-committee/%23:~:text%3Dculminating%2520in%2520the%25201960s%252C%2520a,teachers%2520in%2520the%2520church%2520are&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805662031&amp;usg=AOvVaw3DUDuI4RGLkQYhUpchD7MW">bycommonconsent.com</ref></span><span>. Decentralized &ldquo;rogue&rdquo; sermons and local folklore were largely stamped out, replaced by bland, centrally approved curriculum. In Weberian terms, the Mormon church became a textbook case of the </span><span class="c6">routinization of charisma</span><span>: spiritual spontaneity gave way to </span><span class="c6">legal-rational authority</span><span>&nbsp;and bureaucratic order</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://bycommonconsent.com/2016/04/21/on-the-routinization-bureaucratization-and-correlation-of-charisma-max-weber-and-the-mormons/%23:~:text%3DBut%2520Weber%2520can%2520help%2520us,that%2520are%2520also%2520very%2520real&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805662649&amp;usg=AOvVaw2FcXtjLAyfdBmUT-eR1KHF">bycommonconsent.com</ref></span><span class="c3">.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>By the 1970s the transformation was complete: LDS worship and practice were almost entirely standardized worldwide. Lavish temples and tabernacles proliferated globally, but their rituals and furnishings became homogeneous. The exuberant, apocalyptic message of early leaders &ndash; about common lands, imminent kingdoms, and Adam-God &ndash; was toned down or quietly abandoned. The Church&rsquo;s own historical narratives were sanitized (e.g. polygamy minimized, Adam-God officially denounced</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.fairlatterdaysaints.org/answers/Brigham_Young_and_Adam-God_theory%23:~:text%3DBrigham%2520Young%2520taught%2520that%2520Adam%252C,man%252C%2520was%2520God%2520the%2520Father&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805663381&amp;usg=AOvVaw1qz_HSAIEpvrbMVOv5uuGL">fairlatterdaysaints.org</ref></span><span>). Instead, the focus shifted to </span><span class="c8">individual family and corporate success</span><span class="c3">. In worship services, a modest &ldquo;Restoration&rdquo; message emphasizing the familiar themes of family, faith, and work ethic replaced the old radicalism.</span></p>

=== <span class="c5">Self-Colonization and Neoliberal Accommodation</span> ===
<p class="c0"><span>This institutional drift can be seen as a kind of self-colonization. Once a sect at odds with America, the LDS Church gradually colonized itself by internalizing prevailing bourgeois norms. Kathleen Flake calls the early-20th-century response to the Reed Smoot hearings &ldquo;The Great Accommodation&rdquo;: facing scrutiny, Mormons adopted &ldquo;the terms in which [the nation] would accept Mormonism&rdquo;</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.pbs.org/mormons/themes/accommodation.html%23:~:text%3DMormonism%2527s%2520identity%2520radically%2520changed%2520as,see%2520this%2520in%2520the%2520testimony&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805664402&amp;usg=AOvVaw3JKR-_IB5jasQ5yu4ZGDZx">pbs.org</ref></span><span>. Senator Smoot became the image of the </span><span class="c6">respectable</span><span>&nbsp;Mormon &ndash; a patriotic, business&#8209;suit wearing apostle, not Brigham Young&rsquo;s bearded polygamist avatar</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.pbs.org/mormons/themes/accommodation.html%23:~:text%3DMormonism%2527s%2520identity%2520radically%2520changed%2520as,see%2520this%2520in%2520the%2520testimony&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805664793&amp;usg=AOvVaw1YnOvYsc7WwWIF6jwXE5QQ">pbs.org</ref></span><span>. During WWI and WWII, Mormons &ldquo;over-subscribed&rdquo; their draft quotas to prove they were &ldquo;superpatriotic,&rdquo; recasting themselves as model Americans</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.pbs.org/mormons/themes/accommodation.html%23:~:text%3DThe%2520onset%2520of%2520World%2520War,requiring%252C%2520at%2520the%2520same%2520time&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805665135&amp;usg=AOvVaw3b0uz2wS2vcBdJI0h4sMX3">pbs.org</ref></span><span class="c3">. The Church publicly embraced patriotism, business success, and conservative morality (antivice campaigns), aligning with the mid-century Republican-Protestant consensus. The powerful LDS lobby even argued that Mormon welfare doctrines mirrored New Deal social gospel (rather than critique capitalism).</span></p><p class="c0"><span>Under late 20th-century neoliberalism the accommodation became deeper. Mormon theology ceased to challenge capitalism; in fact, it sanctified free-market virtues. Brighamite wealth and self-reliance became doctrinal cornerstones, and overt class critique vanished. The Church accumulated corporate assets (insurance, real estate, media) and taught members entrepreneurship and home ownership. Social life was organized on family-centered, consumer lines (family home evenings, home building contests, college tuition subsidies) rather than communal sharing. Religious identity became </span><span class="c8">aestheticized</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;and privatized: ritual practice still rich, but its revolutionary edge removed. In Benjaminian terms, what was once a politically charged, communal mythology has turned into a kind of apolitical &ldquo;civil religion&rdquo; &ndash; scripture and temple life lend an aura of sacred order, but the aim is conformity and unity rather than liberation.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>The result is a world&#8209;shrinking LDS trajectory. Where Joseph Smith once envisioned multiple worlds and theocracy, the modern Church offers a world&#8209;now model: local congregations in every nation, a universally rationalized organizational chart, and an emphasis on </span><span class="c8">personal salvation and social conservatism</span><span>. Orthodox Mormonism today reproduces mainstream norms (middle-class domesticity, entrepreneurial drive, bureaucratic governance) far more than it seeks to expand cosmic horizons. The utopian </span><span class="c6">Zion</span><span>&nbsp;has been replaced by ward council meetings; millennial anticipation is channeled into temple attendance quotas. In the language of religious sociology, early Mormonism&rsquo;s </span><span class="c6">maximally enchanted</span><span class="c3">, anti-capitalist orientation has been largely subsumed by a neoliberal-capitalist logic of self-improvement and institutional stability.</span></p><p class="c0"><span>Nonetheless, echoes of the old dispensation survive in the Church&rsquo;s rhetoric of hope and unity. Terms like &ldquo;Zion&rdquo; and &ldquo;eternal progression&rdquo; remain in hymnals, and welfare service recalls communal beginnings. Yet these now coexist with (and often serve) an ethos of conformity. The Mormon journey from </span><span class="c8">world-expanding</span><span>&nbsp;prophet-dream to </span><span class="c8">world-normalizing</span><span class="c3">&nbsp;bureaucracy mirrors a broader pattern: radical religious movements often start by imagining a radically different cosmos, only to end by settling into the contours of the prevailing social order. Early Mormonism&rsquo;s radical cosmic re-enchantment and communal economy gave way, in the era of correlation and globalization, to a corporate structure and aestheticized faith aligned with late modern capitalism. This arc&mdash;from prophets who sought to overthrow old orders to a Church that upholds them&mdash;illustrates both the transformative potential of religion and its capacity for self-domestication in modern society.</span></p><p class="c0"><span class="c8">Sources:</span><span>&nbsp;Scholarly analyses and historical documents on early LDS theology and practice</span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://www.mrm.org/ex-nihilo%23:~:text%3DAccording%2520to%2520LDS%2520teaching%252C%2520finite,is%2520limited%2520by%2520natural%2520law&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805668770&amp;usg=AOvVaw3ejLveZmBe9wQKGK4SJmjq">mrm.org</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://archive.timesandseasons.org/2009/02/mormonism-and-communal-studies/%23:~:text%3DNineteenth,family%2520by%2520embracing%2520plural%2520marriage&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805669002&amp;usg=AOvVaw0KcBG27qH8d6geunv39isW">archive.timesandseasons.org</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Order%23:~:text%3DThe%2520United%2520Order%2520established%2520egalitarian,which&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805669223&amp;usg=AOvVaw0YtjhXqWM4hNtj5Xz1aH8v">en.wikipedia.org</ref></span><span class="c9"><ref>"https://www.google.com/url?q=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Fifty%23:~:text%3D,the%2520Second%2520Coming%2520of%2520Jesus&amp;sa=D&amp;source=editors&amp;ust=1746582805669416&amp;usg=AOvVaw0vUuPfW8CJp4tQl5aOmkc4">en.wikipedia.org</ref></span><span>;
